pronunciation.text: In «детский» the letters «тск» are pronounced «цк»: DYETS-kiy. In «стульчик» the «ль» before «ч» is soft: STOOL'-chik.

translations.en-GB: Do we need to book in advance?
translations.en-US: Do we need to make a reservation?

mnemonic.title: Заранее: before it's early
mnemonic.text: «Заранее» is «за-» (“before”) plus «рано» (“early”): “beforehand”. «Надо» is “must”, the everyday word for what you have to do.

grammar.title: «Надо» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Надо» plus an infinitive means “one has to”: no subject is needed. The verb is imperfective («бронировать») because you ask about the general rule, not one finished booking.

pronunciation.title: Reduced vowels in «заранее»
pronunciation.text: Stress «на», «ни» and «ра»; every other «а» and «о» weakens to a short, unclear “uh”: NA-duh, bruh-NEE-ruh-vuht', zuh-RA-nee-yuh. The final «ть» of «бронировать» is soft.

mnemonic.title: «Boli»: a bully hurts
mnemonic.text: Hear «boli» as “bully”: a bully is the one who hurts you. «Boli mnie…» is literally “it hurts me…”.

grammar.title: Pain hurts «me»
grammar.text: Polish says “hurts me”: «boli mnie» plus the sore part in the nominative, so «gardło», «głowa» (head), «brzuch» (stomach).

pronunciation.title: «ł» is an English w
pronunciation.text: «Ł» is said like English “w”, so «gardło» is “GAR-dwo”. In «mnie» the «m» and «n» blend into one smooth sound.

mnemonic.title: «Lekarz»: the old “leech”
mnemonic.text: «Lekarz» comes from «lek» (medicine). English once had the same idea: a “leech” was a healer, long before the worm.

grammar.title: «Potrzebować» takes the genitive
grammar.text: «Potrzebować» (to need) wants the genitive: «lekarz» becomes «lekarza». Same for «wody» (water), «pomocy» (help).

pronunciation.title: «rz» is a soft zh
pronunciation.text: «Rz» sounds like the «s» in “measure”, so «lekarza» is “leh-KAH-zhah”. The stress is always on the second-to-last syllable.

translations.en-GB: Is there a chemist's around here?
translations.en-US: Is there a pharmacy around here?

mnemonic.title: «Apteka»: the apothecary
mnemonic.text: «Apteka» shares its Greek root with “apothecary”, a place where remedies are stored.

grammar.title: «Czy» opens a yes/no question
grammar.text: Put «czy» at the start and keep the word order: «Jest apteka» (there is a pharmacy) becomes «Czy jest apteka?». No inversion needed.

pronunciation.title: «cz» is a hard “ch”
pronunciation.text: «Cz» is a firmer “ch” than in English, and «y» sounds like the “i” in “bit”. In «gdzieś» say «g» and «dz» together, with no vowel between.

mnemonic.title: «Alergię»: hear “allergy”
mnemonic.text: «Alergia» is “allergy” in Polish clothing. Say it and the doctor will understand at once.

grammar.title: «Mieć … na»: have an allergy to
grammar.text: Polish says “I have an allergy on nuts”: «mam alergię na» plus the accusative plural, «orzechy». Use the same «na» for any allergy.

pronunciation.title: Final «ę» is a soft “eh”
pronunciation.text: At the end of a word «ę» is simply “eh”: «alergię» is “ah-LER-gyeh”. «Ch» is a rasping “h” as in Scottish “loch”.

translations.en-GB: I've had a temperature since yesterday.
translations.en-US: I've had a fever since yesterday.
translations.ru-RU: У меня со вчерашнего дня температура.

mnemonic.title: «Gorączka»: from «gorący», hot
mnemonic.text: «Gorączka» (fever) grows from «gorący» (hot). Hear “go-RON-tsa” and think of a body running hot.

grammar.title: «Od» + «mam»: present for “since”
grammar.text: Polish uses the present tense for something still going on: «od wczoraj mam» is “I have had since yesterday”. «Od» (since, from) takes the genitive.

pronunciation.title: Nasal «ą» sounds like “on”
pronunciation.text: The «ą» is a nasal “on”: «gorączkę» is “go-RON-chkeh”. «Wczoraj» starts with the cluster «fch», so say them in one quick breath.

translations.en-GB: I've got a reservation under the name Kowalski.
translations.en-US: I have a reservation under the name Kowalski.
translations.ru-RU: У меня бронь на фамилию Ковальский.

mnemonic.title: «Rezerwacja»: a reservation with a v
mnemonic.text: «Rezerwacja» is “reservation”, but Polish writes the v sound as «w». Spot it and you have the word.

grammar.title: «Na nazwisko» + surname
grammar.text: «Na nazwisko» (“in the surname”) is followed by the name, which stays unchanged: «na nazwisko Kowalski». «Rezerwacja» becomes «rezerwację» after «mam».

pronunciation.title: «w» is “v”
pronunciation.text: Polish «w» is always “v”: «nazwisko» is “nah-ZVEE-sko”, and «Kowalski» is “ko-VAHL-skee”. «Cj» in «rezerwacja» is “tsy”.

phrases.target: Czy śniadanie jest wliczone w cenę?

translations.en-GB: Is breakfast included in the price?
translations.en-US: Is breakfast included in the price?
translations.bg-BG: Включена ли е закуската в цената?

mnemonic.title: «Śniadanie»: snack at dawn
mnemonic.text: Hear «śniadanie» as “SHNYA-da-nyeh”: a snack-and-dine at the start of the day. It's the first meal.

grammar.title: «W cenę»: accusative after «w»
grammar.text: «Wliczone w cenę» is “counted into the price”: «w» with movement or inclusion takes the accusative, so «cena» becomes «cenę». «Wliczone» agrees with the neuter «śniadanie».

pronunciation.title: «ś» is a soft “sh”
pronunciation.respelling: chih shnya-DAH-nyeh yest vlee-CHO-neh f TSEH-neh
pronunciation.text: «Ś» and «ni» are soft: touch your tongue to the roof of the mouth. Before «c» the «w» in «w cenę» becomes “f”.

translations.en-GB: Could I have the room key, please?
translations.en-US: Could I have the room key, please?
translations.bg-BG: Може ли ключа за стаята, моля?

mnemonic.title: «Klucz»: a clue in your hand
mnemonic.text: «Klucz» sounds like “clue”-ch: the key is the clue that opens the door.

grammar.title: «Poproszę»: the polite request
grammar.text: «Poproszę» (“I'll ask for”) plus the accusative is the polite way to ask for anything: «poproszę klucz», «poproszę wodę». «Do» takes the genitive: «pokój» becomes «pokoju».

pronunciation.title: «cz» and «ó»
pronunciation.text: «Klucz» ends in a hard “ch”, like “klooch”. In «pokoju» the «j» is the English “y”, and «u» is a long “oo”.

translations.bg-BG: В колко часа е освобождаването на стаята?
translations.cs-CZ: V kolik hodin je odhlášení z pokoje?

mnemonic.title: «Wymeldowanie»: “melden” out
mnemonic.text: «Wy-» means out and «meldować» is “to report” (German «melden»): you report yourself out.

grammar.title: «O której»: at which hour
grammar.text: «O której» (“at which”) asks for the time; «o» + locative. The answer repeats it: «o jedenastej» (at eleven). «Której» is the feminine of «który».

pronunciation.title: «ie» is one soft sound
pronunciation.text: «Której» starts with «kt» said as one breath, and «ó» is “oo”. In «wymeldowanie» the «w» is “v” and the stress falls on «-wa-».

phrases.target: W pokoju nie ma ciepłej wody.

translations.en-GB: There's no hot water in the room.
translations.en-US: There's no hot water in the room.

mnemonic.title: «Woda»: the root of vodka
mnemonic.text: «Woda» is water, and «wódka» is literally “little water”. Cold or hot, the root stays.

grammar.title: «Nie ma» + genitive
grammar.text: «Nie ma» (“there is none”) takes the genitive: «woda» becomes «wody» and «ciepła» becomes «ciepłej». Compare «jest woda» with «nie ma wody».

pronunciation.title: «ł» and «w»
pronunciation.respelling: f po-KO-yoo nyeh ma CHEP-wey VO-dih
pronunciation.text: «Ciepłej» has a soft «ć» start and «ł» as English “w”: “CHEP-wey”. At the start «w pokoju» is said “f po-KO-yoo”.

mnemonic.title: «Przymierzyć»: measure
mnemonic.text: «Przymierzyć» hides «miara», “measure”: you measure the clothes against yourself.

grammar.title: «Czy mogę» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Czy mogę…?» (“can I…?”) is followed by a bare infinitive: «mogę to przymierzyć». «Móc» is irregular, so learn «mogę» as it is.

pronunciation.title: «rz» and «przy»
pronunciation.text: «Przy» is “pshih”; the «rz» in «przymierzyć» is “zh”, and the final «ć» is a soft “ch”. Stress the second-to-last syllable.

translations.en-GB: Have you got this in a smaller size?
translations.en-US: Do you have this in a smaller size?
translations.bg-BG: Имате ли това в по-малък размер?

mnemonic.title: «Mniejszy»: mini-er
mnemonic.text: «Mniejszy» (smaller) sounds like “mini”-er: a mini size. It's the comparative of «mały».

grammar.title: «W» + locative
grammar.text: «W» for “in” takes the locative: «rozmiar» becomes «w rozmiarze» and the adjective gets «-ym»: «w mniejszym». «Macie» (you all have) is the friendly shop-floor «wy» form.

pronunciation.title: «mni» is one syllable
pronunciation.text: «Mnie» blends «m» and «n» in one soft beat: “mnyeh”. «Macie» has a soft «ci», like “ch”. The stress in «rozmiarze» is on «-miar-».

mnemonic.title: «Kosztuje»: cost
mnemonic.text: «Kosztuje» begins with «kosz-», the same as English “cost”. Same word, Polish dress.

grammar.title: «Ile»: how much, how many
grammar.text: «Ile» opens “how much” and “how many” questions. The verb «kosztować» (to cost) has no «jest»: «Ile to kosztuje?», or «Ile kosztuje ten sweter?».

pronunciation.title: «sz» is “sh”
pronunciation.text: «Sz» is “sh” and «tu» is a long “oo”. The stress is on «-tu-», the second-to-last syllable.

translations.bg-BG: Мога ли да платя с карта?

mnemonic.title: «Płacić»: pay-wage
mnemonic.text: «Zapłacić» (to pay) begins «zapła-», like “pay-wah”: the till is where you pay.

grammar.title: «Kartą»: instrumental “by means of”
grammar.text: With is «kartą»: «karta» becomes «kartą» (nasal). The instrumental says “with / by”: «kartą», «gotówką» (cash).

pronunciation.title: «ł» and final «ą»
pronunciation.text: «Ł» is “w”: «zapłacić» is “zah-PWAH-cheech”. A final «ą» sounds like “om”.

translations.en-GB: Could I have this one in black?
translations.en-US: Could I have this one in black?
translations.bg-BG: Може ли този в черен цвят?

mnemonic.title: «Czarny»: charcoal black
mnemonic.text: «Czarny» starts like “char”: charcoal is black. Say “char-ny”.

grammar.title: «W kolorze»: locative of colour
grammar.text: After «w», colours take the locative: «kolor» becomes «w kolorze» and «czarny» becomes «czarnym». Say «w czerwonym kolorze» for red.

pronunciation.title: «cz» and final «ze»
pronunciation.text: «Czarnym» opens with a hard “ch” and ends in «ym», like “im” in “him”. «Kolorze» has «rz» = “zh”.

mnemonic.title: «Słychać»: what's audible
mnemonic.text: «Słychać» means “is heard”: you are asking “what is heard from you?”. Hear “SWIH-hach”: news you can listen to.

grammar.title: «U ciebie»: at your place
grammar.text: «U» + genitive means “at someone's”: «u ciebie» (at yours). So «Co u ciebie słychać?» is “what's audible at yours?”. A formal version is «Co u pana słychać?».

pronunciation.title: «ł» is a “w”
pronunciation.text: «Ł» is “w”: «słychać» is “SWIH-hach”. «Ch» is a light rasp and the final «ć» a soft “ch”.

mnemonic.title: «Imię»: a cousin of «имя»
mnemonic.text: If you know Russian «имя» or Latin “nomen”, then «imię» is the same family: the word for name.

grammar.title: «Na imię»: a fixed phrase
grammar.text: Polish asks “how do you have for name?”: «Jak masz na imię?». Answer «Mam na imię Anna» or «Jestem Anna». «Masz» is informal; formal: «Jak się pan nazywa?».

pronunciation.title: Nasal «ę» at the end
pronunciation.text: «Imię» ends in «ę», which at the end of a word is a plain “eh”. «Masz» ends in «sz»: “mash”.

translations.en-US: This is my first time here.

mnemonic.title: «Pierwszy»: first, like “prime”
mnemonic.text: «Pierwszy» (first) and English “prime” share a distant root: the one that comes first.

grammar.title: «Jestem»: no «ja» needed
grammar.text: Polish drops the subject pronoun because «jestem» already means “I am”. «Pierwszy raz» (first time) has no preposition: just two words.

pronunciation.title: «rsz» cluster
pronunciation.text: «Pierwszy» packs «rw» then «sz»: say “PYER-shih”. «Jestem» starts with “y”.

mnemonic.title: «Mieszkanie»: me in my place
mnemonic.text: «Mieszkanie» (a flat) starts with “me”: picture yourself at home in your own flat. Where you have your «mieszkanie» is where you «mieszkasz» (live).

grammar.title: «Gdzie» + present tense
grammar.text: «Gdzie» (where) is followed by the verb: «mieszkam» (I live), «mieszkasz» (you live). Answer with «w» + locative: «mieszkam w Londynie».

pronunciation.title: «sz» and «ie»
pronunciation.text: «Gdzie» starts with «g» and «dz» without a vowel. In «mieszkasz» the «sz» is “sh”, and «ie» is “ye”: “MYESH-kash”.

mnemonic.title: «Mówić»: move your mouth
mnemonic.text: Hear «mówić» as “MOO-veech”: move your mouth, and you are speaking.

grammar.title: «Po» + adverb for languages
grammar.text: Languages after «mówić» use «po»: «po angielsku», «po polsku», «po hiszpańsku». They are lower-case adverbs ending in «-sku»; ask politely with «Czy pan mówi...?».

pronunciation.title: «ó» is “oo”
pronunciation.text: «Ó» is the same as «u»: “oo”. «Ang-» has a nasal «n» before «g», and «ie» is “ye”: “ahn-GYEL-skoo”.

mnemonic.title: «Gorąco»: go, run, so hot
mnemonic.text: Hear «gorąco» as “go-RON-tso”: go and run, it's so hot. It's the hot of weather.

grammar.title: Weather uses «jest» + adverb
grammar.text: Polish says the weather with «jest» and an adverb: «jest gorąco», «jest zimno». No adjective, no «it».

pronunciation.title: «dz» is one sound
pronunciation.text: «Dz» is one sound, like “ds” in “beds”. «Dzisiaj» starts with soft «dzi», like “jee”.

mnemonic.title: «Pada»: rain pads down
mnemonic.text: Hear «pada» as “pad”: rain pads down. It literally means “falls”.

grammar.title: «Padać»: rain “falls”
grammar.text: Rain and snow «fall» in Polish: «pada deszcz», «pada śnieg». The verb is always third person singular, like «pada»; no «it» is needed.

pronunciation.title: «szcz» = “shch”
pronunciation.text: «Szcz» is a double hush like “sh-ch” in “fresh cheese”: «deszcz» is “deshch”. «P» has no puff of air, softer than English.

translations.en-GB: What will the weather be like tomorrow?
translations.en-US: What will the weather be like tomorrow?

mnemonic.title: «Pogoda»: a pagoda of weather
mnemonic.text: Hear «pogoda» as “pagoda”: picture a pagoda under the sky. It means weather.

grammar.title: «Będzie»: future of «być»
grammar.text: «Będzie» is “will be”, the future of «być». The question word «jaka» agrees with the feminine «pogoda»: «jaka pogoda?» (what weather?).

pronunciation.title: «ę» before «d»
pronunciation.text: The «ę» before «d» is “en”: «będzie» is “BEN-jeh”. «Jutro» starts with “y”.

translations.en-GB: It's cold and the wind's blowing.

mnemonic.title: «Zimno»: from «zima», winter
mnemonic.text: «Zimno» (cold) grows out of «zima» (winter): winter-ish. Hear “ZHEEM-no”.

grammar.title: «Wiatr wieje»: the wind blows
grammar.text: The wind «wieje» (blows): «wiatr wieje». Weather again uses «jest» + adverb: «jest zimno». The word «i» just means “and”.

pronunciation.title: «wiatr» cluster
pronunciation.text: «Ź» is a soft “zh”. «Wiatr» is one syllable: “vyatr”, and the «tr» at the end is said sharply.

translations.en-GB: Take an umbrella, it's going to rain.
translations.en-US: Take an umbrella, it's going to rain.

mnemonic.title: «Parasol»: a shade for sun and rain
mnemonic.text: «Parasol» is English “parasol”, a sun shade, and Polish also uses it for a rain umbrella.

grammar.title: «Weź» is an irregular command
grammar.text: «Brać» (to take) has a command «weź» (take!). «Bo» (because) is the everyday spoken «because». «Będzie padać» is the future “it will fall”.

pronunciation.title: «ź» is a soft “zh”
pronunciation.text: «Weź» ends in a soft «ź» that devoices to “sh”. «Parasol» stresses «-ra-»: “pah-RAH-sol”.

translations.en-GB: What are you doing at the weekend?
translations.en-US: What are you doing this weekend?

mnemonic.title: «Robić»: where “robot” comes from
mnemonic.text: The word “robot” comes from Czech «robota» (work), a cousin of Polish «robić» (to do): a robot is a “doer”.

grammar.title: Present tense for plans
grammar.text: Polish uses the present for near plans: «Co robisz w weekend?» is “what do you do at the weekend?”. «W» + accusative is “on / at” a day: «w weekend», «w piątek».

pronunciation.title: «c» is “ts”
pronunciation.text: «Co» is “tso” (a «c» is always “ts”). «Weekend» keeps its English spelling, but «w» is “v”: say “VEE-kend”.

translations.en-GB: Do you fancy going to the cinema?
translations.en-US: Do you feel like going to the movies?
translations.bg-BG: Искаш ли да отидем на кино?

mnemonic.title: «Ochota»: oh, HOT desire
mnemonic.text: Hear «ochota» as “oh-HO-ta”: hot desire. «Masz ochotę» is “do you have the wish”.

grammar.title: «Masz ochotę» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Mieć ochotę» (to feel like) is followed by an infinitive: «masz ochotę pójść?». «Do» takes the genitive: «kino» becomes «kina».

pronunciation.title: «ó» and «ść»
pronunciation.text: «Ó» is “oo”. «Ść» is a soft “shch”: «pójść» is “pooysht”, said as one quick syllable.

mnemonic.title: «Spotkać»: spot to meet
mnemonic.text: «Spotkać się» holds “spot”: you meet at a spot. It's an easy hook.

grammar.title: «-my»: let's
grammar.text: The ending «-my» turns a verb into “let's”: «spotkajmy się». «O» + locative + a feminine ordinal gives the hour: «o ósmej» (at eight).

pronunciation.title: «ó» and «sm»
pronunciation.text: «Ó» in «ósmej» is “oo” and «sm» goes together: “OOS-mey”. «Się» is a soft “sheh”.

translations.bg-BG: За съжаление не мога в петък.
translations.ru-RU: К сожалению, в пятницу не могу.

mnemonic.title: «Piątek»: the fifth day
mnemonic.text: «Piątek» (Friday) comes from «pięć» (five): Friday is the fifth day of the Polish week.

grammar.title: «Nie» + verb
grammar.text: «Nie» before the verb makes it negative: «mogę» becomes «nie mogę». «W» + accusative for days: «w piątek».

pronunciation.title: Nasal «ą»
pronunciation.text: In «piątek» the «ą» sounds like “on”: “PYON-tek”. «W» before a voiceless «p» is “f”.

mnemonic.title: «Raz»: once, and «razem»: together
mnemonic.text: «Raz» is “once” (a time); «razem» also means “together”. Here “another once”.

grammar.title: Fixed phrase in the instrumental
grammar.text: «Innym razem» (another time) is a set phrase: noun and adjective both take the instrumental, «-em» and «-ym». «Może» alone means “maybe”.

pronunciation.title: «rz» and «ż» are “zh”
pronunciation.text: «Może» has «ż» = “zh”: “MO-zheh”. «Nn» in «innym» is held a little longer.

mnemonic.title: «Odprawa»: dispatch off
mnemonic.text: «Odprawa» is a “dispatch”: «od-» (away) + «prawa» (set right). You are sent on your way.

grammar.title: «Gdzie jest» + noun
grammar.text: «Gdzie jest…?» (where is) is followed by the nominative: «odprawa», «wyjście». No article, no «the».

pronunciation.title: «gdzie» is a cluster
pronunciation.text: «Gdzie» starts with «g» + «dz» with no vowel: “GDJEH”. In «odprawa» the «d» turns into “t”.

translations.ru-RU: Как пройти к выходу номер пять?
translations.cs-CZ: Kudy se jde k východu číslo pět?

mnemonic.title: «Wyjście»: way out
mnemonic.text: «Wyjście» is “way out”: «wy-» (out) + «jść» (to go). The gate is the going-out.

grammar.title: «Do» + genitive
grammar.text: «Do» (to) takes the genitive: «wyjście» becomes «wyjścia». «Numer pięć» needs no «of»: noun, then number.

pronunciation.title: «którędy» and «ść»
pronunciation.text: «Kt» goes together in one breath: “ktoo”. «Ść» in «wyjścia» is a soft “shch”. «Pięć» ends in a soft «ć».

mnemonic.title: «Lot»: a lot of sky
mnemonic.text: «Lot» (flight) rhymes with English “lot”: picture a whole lot of sky. It is the same root as in «lotnisko», airport.

grammar.title: Adjectives match the noun
grammar.text: «Mój» and «opóźniony» are masculine to agree with «lot». For a feminine noun use «moja» and «opóźniona»: «moja podróż jest opóźniona».

pronunciation.title: «ó» and «ź»
pronunciation.text: «Mój» is “mooy” and «ó» in «opóźniony» is “oo”. «Ź» is a soft “zh”.

mnemonic.title: «Bagaż»: baggage
mnemonic.text: «Bagaż» is “baggage”: both come from Old French. The «ż» is just “zh”.

grammar.title: Past tense matches gender
grammar.text: The past adds «-ł» for masculine: «dotarł». A feminine subject would be «dotarła»: «walizka nie dotarła». Compare «bagaż» (masc.) and «walizka» (a suitcase, fem.).

pronunciation.title: Final «ż» sounds like “sh”
pronunciation.text: A final «ż» is devoiced to “sh”: «bagaż» is “BAH-gash”. The «ł» in «dotarł» is a “w”.

translations.en-GB: Could I have a window seat, please?
translations.en-US: Could I have a window seat, please?

mnemonic.title: «Okno»: a little eye
mnemonic.text: «Okno» comes from «oko» (eye): a window is an eye in the wall.

grammar.title: «Przy» + locative
grammar.text: «Przy» (by, next to) takes the locative: «okno» becomes «oknie». «Miejsce» is a neuter noun, so «miejsce przy oknie» is “a seat by the window”.

pronunciation.title: «przy» and «ie»
pronunciation.text: «Przy» is “pshih”. In «miejsce» say «j» as “y” and the double «s-tse»; «oknie» is “OK-nyeh”.

mnemonic.title: «Pomóc»: “pomoc” is help
mnemonic.text: Say «po-MOOTS» and picture “pal, more!” — a friend you call for «pomoc», help.

grammar.title: «Pomóc» takes the dative
grammar.text: «Pomóc» (to help) takes the dative: «mi» (to me), not «mnie». «Proszę» + infinitive is “please do”: «proszę mi pomóc».

pronunciation.title: «ó» is “oo”
pronunciation.text: «Ó» is “oo” and the final «c» is “ts”: «pomóc» is “PO-moots”. «Proszę» has «sz» = “sh”.

mnemonic.title: «Rozum»: reason inside
mnemonic.text: «Rozumiem» hides «rozum» (mind, reason): you are reasoning with it, so you understand.

grammar.title: «Nie» + verb
grammar.text: Make any verb negative with «nie»: «rozumiem» becomes «nie rozumiem». The verb is conjugated: «rozumiesz» (you understand), «rozumie» (he understands).

pronunciation.title: «rz» is not in it
pronunciation.text: «Nie» is “nyeh”, one soft syllable. The stress is on the long «u»: “ro-ZOO-myem”.

mnemonic.title: «Powtórzyć»: a second time
mnemonic.text: «Powtórzyć» hides «wtór» (second): do it a second time. Very close to “repeat”.

grammar.title: «Pan» / «pani»: formal “you”
grammar.text: Polish is formal with «pan» (to a man) and «pani» (to a woman), plus the third person: «Czy może pan powtórzyć?». Use «możesz» with friends.

pronunciation.title: «wt» and «rz»
pronunciation.text: «Powtórzyć» has «w» = “f” before «t»: “pof-TOO-zhich”. «Ó» is “oo”, «rz» is “zh”.

mnemonic.title: «Dzwon»: a bell
mnemonic.text: «Dzwonić» comes from «dzwon» (bell): to ring a bell is to phone.

grammar.title: «Na» + accusative
grammar.text: «Na» for a call to a service takes the accusative: «policja» becomes «policję». «Zadzwoń» is the command (informal): «zadzwoń!».

pronunciation.title: «dzw» cluster
pronunciation.text: «Dz» is one sound: “dz”. «Zadzwoń» ends in a soft «ń», like “ny”. «Policję» ends in an «ę»: “eh”.

translations.en-GB: I don't know where I am.
translations.en-US: I don't know where I am.

mnemonic.title: «Wiem»: wit
mnemonic.text: «Wiem» (I know) matches English “wit”, as in “to wit” and “wisdom”.

grammar.title: «Nie wiem» + question word
grammar.text: After «nie wiem» the question word follows directly, with no “that”: «nie wiem, gdzie jestem», «nie wiem, co to jest».

pronunciation.title: «wiem» is one syllable
pronunciation.text: «Wiem» is one syllable, “vyem”. «Gdzie» is “gdjeh” with no vowel between «g» and «dz».

mnemonic.title: «Biuro»: a bureau
mnemonic.text: «Biuro» is “bureau”: both come from French. Polish writes it «biuro».

grammar.title: «W» + locative
grammar.text: «W» (in) takes the locative: «biuro» becomes «w biurze» (the «r» softens to «rz»). «Pracuję» is “I work”.

pronunciation.title: «c» is “ts”
pronunciation.text: «Pracuję» has «c» = “ts”: “prah-TSOO-yeh”. «Biurze» is “BYOO-zheh” with «rz» = “zh”.

translations.en-GB: I've got a meeting at ten.
translations.en-US: I have a meeting at ten.

mnemonic.title: «Dziesiąta»: ten, like “decimal”
mnemonic.text: «Dziesiąta» (tenth) is like “decimal”: both mean ten. «Spotkanie» holds “spot”: a meeting at a spot.

grammar.title: «O» + locative: at an hour
grammar.text: Hours use ordinals: «o dziesiątej» is “at the tenth (hour)”, feminine locative «-ej». So «o ósmej», «o pierwszej».

pronunciation.title: Nasal «ą» + soft «dzi»
pronunciation.text: «Dzie» is a soft “jeh”, «sią» is “shon”: «dziesiątej» is “jeh-SHON-tey”. «Spotkanie» is stressed on «-ka-».

mnemonic.title: «Wyślę»: send out
mnemonic.text: «Wy-» is “out” and «ślę» is “send”: you send it out. Same «wy-» as in «wyjście».

grammar.title: Perfective = future
grammar.text: «Wyślę» is perfective, so its present form already means “I will send”: no «będę» is needed. «Ci» is the short “to you”: «wyślę ci».

pronunciation.title: «ś» is a soft “sh”
pronunciation.text: «Wyślę» has a soft «ś» = “sh” then «l»: “VIH-shleh”. «Ci» is “chee”.

translations.en-GB: I've got a lot of work.
translations.en-US: I have a lot of work.

mnemonic.title: «Dużo»: a doozy
mnemonic.text: Hear «dużo» as “DOO-zho”: a doozy of a pile. It means “a lot”.

grammar.title: «Dużo» + genitive
grammar.text: «Dużo» (a lot) takes the genitive: «praca» becomes «pracy». The same for «dużo wody», «dużo czasu».

pronunciation.title: «ż» is “zh”
pronunciation.text: «Ż» is “zh”, as in “measure”: “DOO-zho”. «Pracy» is “PRAH-tsih”.

mnemonic.title: «Przerwa»: a tear in the day
mnemonic.text: «Przerwa» (break) comes from «rwać» (to tear): a tear in the working day.

grammar.title: «Na» + accusative: for
grammar.text: «Na» + accusative gives a purpose, “for”: «przerwa na lunch», «czas na kawę». «Przerwa» becomes «przerwę».

pronunciation.title: «przerwę»: «rz» sound
pronunciation.text: «Prze» is “pshe”; «w» is “v”. «Lunch» is borrowed, so it's said “lanch”.

mnemonic.title: «Halo»: same as “hello”
mnemonic.text: «Halo» is the phone “hello” in Polish and in nearly every language. It's the easiest word of all.

grammar.title: «Kto» + third person
grammar.text: «Kto» (who) takes the third person singular: «kto mówi?» (who is speaking?). Same for «kto dzwoni?» (who is calling?).

pronunciation.title: «h» is a rasp
pronunciation.text: «H» is a light rasp like “ch” in “loch”. «Kto» is one breath, “kto”. «Mówi» has «ó» = “oo”.

mnemonic.title: «Hasło»: a hassle-o
mnemonic.text: Hear «hasło» as “hassle-o”: a password can be a hassle to remember.

grammar.title: «Jakie» agrees with the noun
grammar.text: «Jakie» (what kind of) matches the neuter «hasło». For a feminine noun use «jaka»: «jaka jest pogoda?». «Do» takes the genitive: «do wifi».

pronunciation.title: «ł» is a “w”
pronunciation.text: «Ł» is a “w”: «hasło» is “HAH-swo”. «Wifi» is said “VEE-fee”, with «w» = “v”.

mnemonic.title: «Ładować»: to load
mnemonic.text: «Ładować» is “to load”: charging is loading power. «Rozładować» is “unload”, so it's flat.

grammar.title: «Się»: it happens by itself
grammar.text: «Się» shows it happened to the thing itself: «rozładował się» is “got unloaded”. The past ends in «-ł» because «telefon» is masculine.

pronunciation.title: «ł» is “w”
pronunciation.text: «Ł» is “w”: «rozładował» is “roz-wah-DO-vaw”. «Telefon» is stressed on «-le-».

mnemonic.title: «Ładowarka»: the loader
mnemonic.text: «Ładowarka» is the “loader”: «ładować» (load) + «-arka» (a thing that does it). Charger.

grammar.title: «Mieć» + accusative
grammar.text: After «mieć» (to have) a feminine noun takes the accusative: «ładowarka» becomes «ładowarkę». «Czy» starts the question.

pronunciation.title: «ł» and «rk»
pronunciation.text: «Ł» is “w”: «ładowarkę» is “wah-do-VAR-keh”. The stress is on «-war-».

mnemonic.title: «Oddzwonić»: ring back
mnemonic.text: «Od-» is “back” and «dzwonić» is “ring”: ring back. Same «dzwon» as in «zadzwoń».

grammar.title: «Do» + genitive of «ty»
grammar.text: After «do» the pronoun is genitive: «ty» becomes «ciebie». «Później» (later) stays the same: «później», «wcześniej» (earlier).

pronunciation.title: «dzw» cluster
pronunciation.text: The double «dd» in «oddzwonię» is held a little longer. «Ciebie» starts with a soft «ci» = “ch”; «ź» is a soft “zh”.

mnemonic.title: «Żona»: Joan
mnemonic.text: Hear «żona» as “ZHO-na”, a bit like “Joan”: picture your wife Joan.

grammar.title: «Moja» matches the noun
grammar.text: The word «moja» (my) matches the feminine «żona». For a husband, «mój mąż» (masculine). «To jest» introduces someone: “this is”.

pronunciation.title: «ż» is “zh”
pronunciation.text: «Ż» is “zh” as in “measure”: “ZHO-na”. «Moja» has «j» = “y”: “MO-ya”.

mnemonic.title: «Dzieci»: dzieci = jeh-chee
mnemonic.text: Hear «dzieci» as “JEH-chee”: children. It is always plural, a group.

grammar.title: «Dwoje», not «dwa»
grammar.text: For children and mixed groups Polish uses collective numbers: «dwoje», «troje». Not «dwa dzieci». «Dwoje dzieci» is “a two of children”.

pronunciation.title: «dzie» is soft “jeh”
pronunciation.text: «Dzieci» starts with a soft «dz» = “j”: “JEH-chee”. «Dwoje» is “DVO-yeh”.

mnemonic.title: «Brat»: a brat
mnemonic.text: «Brat» is “brother”, and English has “brat”: the little rascal of the family.

grammar.title: Masculine animate: accusative = genitive
grammar.text: For masculine people the accusative looks like the genitive: «brat» becomes «brata», «starszy» becomes «starszego». That's after «mieć» (to have).

pronunciation.title: «rsz» in a row
pronunciation.text: «Starszego» packs «rsz»: “star-SHEH-go”. «G» is hard, as in “go”.

mnemonic.title: «Rodzice»: from «rodzić»
mnemonic.text: «Rodzice» comes from «rodzić» (to give birth): the parents are the givers of birth. «Rod» also means “family line”.

grammar.title: «Moi» for people, plural
grammar.text: «Moi» is “my” for masculine-personal plural, so «rodzice» takes «moi». «W» + locative: «Kraków» becomes «w Krakowie».

pronunciation.title: «dz» and «sz»
pronunciation.text: «Rodzice» has a soft «dz» = “j”: “ro-JEE-tseh”. A final «-ą» sounds like “om”: “myesh-KAH-yom”.

translations.bg-BG: Синът ми е на пет години.

mnemonic.title: «Syn»: a little sin
mnemonic.text: «Syn» sounds like “sin” but means “son”: the family joke is that a son is a little “sin”.

grammar.title: Age with «mieć»
grammar.text: Age uses «mieć» (to have): «ma pięć lat» is “has five years”. After 5 and above Polish uses «lat», not «lata»: «ma dwa lata» but «ma pięć lat».

pronunciation.title: Nasal «ę» before «ć»
pronunciation.text: «Syn» has «y» like the “i” in “bit”. In «pięć» the «ę» becomes “en”: “pyench”.

phrases.target: Chciałbym zarezerwować stolik na cztery osoby.

translations.en-GB: I'd like to book a table for four people.
translations.en-US: I'd like to reserve a table for four.
translations.bg-BG: Бих искал да запазя маса за четирима.
translations.ru-RU: Я хотел бы забронировать столик на четверых.
translations.cs-CZ: Chtěl bych rezervovat stůl pro čtyři osoby.

mnemonic.title: «Stolik»: a little stool
mnemonic.text: «Stolik» is a little «stół» (table). Hear “stool”: a small table.

grammar.title: «Chciałbym»: I'd like
grammar.text: «Chciałbym» is “I would like” for a man; a woman says «chciałabym». «Zarezerwować» follows as an infinitive. «Na» + number + «osoby».

pronunciation.title: «chc» cluster
pronunciation.respelling: HCHAW-bim za-reh-zer-VO-vach STO-leek na CHTEH-rih o-SO-bih
pronunciation.text: «Chciałbym» starts with a rasp «ch» then «ć»: “HCHAW-bim”. «Ł» is “w”. «Cztery» is “CHTEH-rih”.

phrases.target: Czy jest wolny stolik na dziś wieczorem?

translations.en-GB: Is there a table free this evening?
translations.en-US: Do you have a table free tonight?
translations.bg-BG: Има ли свободна маса тази вечер?
translations.ru-RU: Есть свободный столик на сегодня вечером?

mnemonic.title: «Wolny»: free, at will
mnemonic.text: «Wolny» sounds like “volny” and means free: at your own will. Also «wolność» is freedom.

grammar.title: «Wieczorem»: instrumental of time
grammar.text: Parts of the day take the instrumental: «wieczorem» (in the evening), «rano» (in the morning). With «dziś» it means “this evening”.

pronunciation.title: «w» is “v”
pronunciation.ipa: [tʂɨ jɛst ˈvɔlnɨ ˈstɔlik na dʑiɕ vjɛˈtʂɔrɛm]
pronunciation.respelling: chih yest VOL-nih STO-leek na jeesh vyeh-CHO-rem
pronunciation.text: «Wolny» starts with “v”. «Dziś» is a soft “jeesh”, «wieczorem» is “vyeh-CHO-rem”.

translations.en-GB: A table on the terrace, please.
translations.en-US: A table on the patio, please.

mnemonic.title: «Taras»: a terrace
mnemonic.text: «Taras» is “terrace”: the same word, shorter. Easy to remember.

grammar.title: «Na» + locative
grammar.text: «Na» (on) takes the locative: «taras» becomes «na tarasie» (the «s» turns soft). Compare «na dworze» (outside).

pronunciation.title: «si» is a soft “sh”
pronunciation.text: «Tarasie» has a soft «si» = “sh”: “ta-RAH-sheh”. «Poproszę» has «sz» = “sh”.

translations.en-GB: I want to cancel my reservation.
translations.en-US: I want to cancel my reservation.

mnemonic.title: «Odwołać»: call off
mnemonic.text: «Odwołać» is “call off”: «od-» (off) + «wołać» (to call). Same idea as English.

grammar.title: «Chcę» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Chcę» (I want) is followed by an infinitive: «chcę odwołać». «Rezerwacja» becomes «rezerwację» (accusative).

pronunciation.title: «chcę»: harsh «ch»
pronunciation.text: «Chcę» is a rasp «h» + «ts» + «eh»: “htseh”. In «odwołać» «ł» is “w”: “od-VO-wach”.

translations.en-GB: I'm booking a table for a birthday.
translations.en-US: I'm booking a table for a birthday.

mnemonic.title: «Urodziny»: birth-days
mnemonic.text: «Urodziny» comes from «rodzić» (give birth), the same root as «rodzice». It is the birth-day.

grammar.title: «Urodziny» is always plural
grammar.text: «Urodziny» (birthday) is plural-only: «na urodziny» (for a birthday), «wszystkiego najlepszego z okazji urodzin» when wishing. «Rezerwuję» is “I'm booking”.

pronunciation.title: «dz» is soft “j”
pronunciation.text: «Dzi» is a soft “j”: «urodziny» is “oo-ro-JEE-nih”. «Rezerwuję» has «w» = “v”.

mnemonic.title: Bolí: a ball to the head
mnemonic.text: «Bolí» (it hurts) sounds like “ball-ee”: picture a ball hitting your head. It is the same root as Bulgarian «боли».

grammar.title: The sore part is the subject
grammar.text: Czech says “the head hurts me”: «mě» is “me” and «hlava» is the thing that hurts. Swap the noun for another body part: «Bolí mě záda» (my back hurts).

pronunciation.title: Soft h, and «mě» is “mnyeh”
pronunciation.text: «H» is a light breath, softer than English “h”. After «m», the «ě» turns the sound into «mnyeh». The stress is always on the first syllable: BOH-lee, HLAH-va.

translations.en-GB: I need something for a cough
translations.en-US: I need something for a cough

mnemonic.title: Lék: a leek soup remedy
mnemonic.text: «Lék» (medicine) sounds like “leek”: picture a bowl of leek soup as grandma’s cure. Related: «lékárna» (pharmacy) and «lékař» (doctor).

grammar.title: «Na» + accusative: for what
grammar.text: «Na» plus the accusative names what a remedy is for: «lék na kašel», «lék na bolest» (for pain). «Potřebuju» is the spoken form of «potřebuji» (I need).

pronunciation.title: The Czech ř
pronunciation.text: «Ř» is a rolled «r» and a «zh» said together; start with «rzh» and relax into it. «Lék» has a long vowel: hold it a beat. «Š» is «sh».

mnemonic.title: Alergický: allergic, nearly
mnemonic.text: «Alergický» is “allergic” with a Czech ending: you already know the word. «Ořechy» (nuts) is the one new thing to remember.

grammar.title: Adjectives match the speaker
grammar.text: A man says «alergický», a woman says «alergická». After «na», the thing you react to goes in the accusative plural: «ořechy». Also: «na lepek» (gluten).

pronunciation.title: Jsem sounds like “sem”
pronunciation.text: In «jsem» the «j» is almost silent: say “sem”. The «ch» in «ořechy» is a throaty «h» like in Scottish “loch”. Stress is on the first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Horečka: hot, hot
mnemonic.text: «Horečka» (fever) starts like “hot”: picture a hot forehead. It comes from «hořet», to burn.

grammar.title: «Mám» + accusative
grammar.text: «Mám» means “I have” and the thing you have takes the accusative: «horečka» → «horečku», «rýma» → «rýmu» (a cold). Czech does not need «já» (I).

pronunciation.title: Long á, soft «če»
pronunciation.text: The «á» in «mám» is long: hold it. «Č» is «ch» as in “church”, so «horečku» is HOR-etch-koo. Stress goes on the first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Zavolejte: voice call
mnemonic.text: «Zavolejte» holds «volat» (to call), like “vocal”: you use your voice to call. «Lékař» is the doctor, from «lék» (medicine).

grammar.title: Polite orders end in «-te»
grammar.text: The «-te» ending makes a polite command to «vy»: «zavolejte», «počkejte» (wait). A doctor, as the thing you call, is in the accusative: «lékař» → «lékaře».

pronunciation.title: Long é and í
pronunciation.text: Hold the long vowels in «lékaře» and «prosím» a little longer than the short ones. «Ř» is «r» and «zh» together. Stress: first syllable of each word.

translations.en-GB: I've got a booking under the name Novák
translations.en-US: I have a reservation under the name Novák
translations.ru-RU: У меня бронь на фамилию Новак

mnemonic.title: Rezervaci: reservation
mnemonic.text: «Rezervaci» is “reservation” with a Czech ending, so you can guess it. «Jméno» (name) is the new word to keep.

grammar.title: «Na» + accusative: under a name
grammar.text: «Na jméno» means “under the name”. «Rezervace» changes to «rezervaci» because it is what you have (accusative). The surname stays as it is: «Novák».

pronunciation.title: «Jm» at the start
pronunciation.text: «Jméno» begins with a quick «y» and straight into «m»: no vowel between. The «c» in «rezervaci» is «ts». Stress: first syllable.

translations.en-GB: Is there air conditioning in the room?
translations.en-US: Is there air conditioning in the room?

mnemonic.title: Pokoj: peace and a room
mnemonic.text: «Pokoj» means both “room” and “peace”: a hotel room is a place of peace. Russian «покой» is the same word.

grammar.title: «V» + locative: in the room
grammar.text: «V» (in) puts the noun into the locative: «pokoj» → «v pokoji». Czech asks “is there…?” with just «je»: no «there» needed. Order: «Je … klimatizace?».

pronunciation.title: Stress first, «c» is ts
pronunciation.text: «V» before «p» is said as «f»: «f pokoji». The «c» in «klimatizace» is «ts». Czech stress is on the first syllable: POH-ko-yi.

mnemonic.title: Noc: la noche, ночь, night
mnemonic.text: «Noc» is built like «noche», «ночь» and “night”: one short word, and it ends the same way as Russian «ночь».

grammar.title: «Stojí»: “it stands”, so it costs
grammar.text: «Stojí» literally means “stands”: the price “stands” at some amount. «Kolik» is “how much/how many”. Say «jedna» for “one” with a feminine noun: «jedna noc».

pronunciation.title: Stress and a final ts
pronunciation.text: «C» at the end of «noc» is «ts», like the end of “cats”. «Stojí» has a long final «í». Stress: first syllable of each word.

translations.en-GB: Can I leave my luggage here?
translations.en-US: Can I leave my bags here?
translations.bg-BG: Мога ли да оставя багажа си тук?

mnemonic.title: Zavazadla: za + bags
mnemonic.text: «Zavazadla» (luggage) comes from «vázat» (to tie): luggage is what you tie up and pack. Picture a strap around a bag.

grammar.title: «Můžu» and the infinitive
grammar.text: «Můžu» (I can) is followed by an infinitive at the end: «nechat» (leave). «Si» is a small word that means “for myself”, it sits second in the sentence: «Můžu si tady nechat…».

pronunciation.title: The long ů
pronunciation.text: «Ů» is a long «u», the same as «ú»: «moo». «Ž» is «zh», as in “measure”. «Ch» in «nechat» is a breathy «h». Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Snídaně: a sneaky breakfast
mnemonic.text: «Snídaně» starts with “snee”: picture sneaking down early for the first breakfast. The root is Slavic «sъn-» like Polish «śniadanie».

grammar.title: «V kolik»: at what time
grammar.text: «V kolik» means “at what time?” and the answer uses «v» too: «v osm» (at eight). «Je» (is) comes after the question, and the thing you ask about sits at the end.

pronunciation.title: Soft «ně», long «í»
pronunciation.text: «V» before «k» is said as «f». The «í» in «snídaně» is long, and «ně» is a soft «nye». Stress: first syllable of «snídaně».

mnemonic.title: Zkusit: scooting it on
mnemonic.text: «Zkusit» sounds like “skoo-sit”: picture scooting into a jacket to test it. It means “to try”, in any situation.

grammar.title: «Si» for your own body
grammar.text: «Zkusit si» means to try something on yourself: «si» marks it as for you. «To» is “it/this”. Same pattern: «Můžu si to vzít?» (can I take it?).

pronunciation.title: Z before k sounds like s
pronunciation.text: Spelling «zk» is read «sk»: Czech makes a voiced sound voiceless before a voiceless one. «Ů» is a long «u». Stress: first syllable.

translations.en-GB: Do you have a bigger size?
translations.en-US: Do you have a bigger size?

mnemonic.title: Velikost: very large
mnemonic.text: «Velikost» (size) shares a root with «veliký» (great, huge): Bulgarian «велик» and Russian «великий». Think “very large”.

grammar.title: «Větší»: an irregular comparative
grammar.text: «Větší» (bigger) comes from «velký» (big), and is irregular like English “good → better”. For smaller: «menší». «Máte…?» is the plain way to ask “do you have…?”.

pronunciation.title: «Vě» is “vyeh”
pronunciation.text: «Ě» after «v» gives «vye», so «větší» is VYET-shee. The «tš» in «větší» runs together as «ch». Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Kabinky: little cabins
mnemonic.text: «Kabinky» looks like “cabins”: fitting rooms are little cabins with a curtain. The ending «-ky» makes it plural.

grammar.title: «Jsou»: are
grammar.text: «Jsou» is “are” for plural things: «Kde jsou kabinky?». For one room it is «Kde je kabinka?». «Kde» (where) opens the question and the verb follows.

pronunciation.title: Silent j in «jsou»
pronunciation.text: In «jsou» the «j» is almost silent: say “sow” (rhymes with “cow”). «Kde» is «gde». In «kabinky», «n» before «k» sounds like «ng». Stress: first syllable of «kabinky».

translations.en-GB: This is too big for me
translations.en-US: This is too big for me
translations.pl-PL: To jest dla mnie za duże

mnemonic.title: Moc: “much”, with a ts
mnemonic.text: «Moc» (too, very) sounds like “mots”: think “too much”. Same word as «moc» (power) in Russian «мощь».

grammar.title: «Mi» and neuter «velké»
grammar.text: «Je mi…» is “it is … for me”, literally “to me”. «Velké» ends in «-é» because «tohle» (this, neuter) is neuter. Say «velký» for a masculine thing, «velká» for a feminine one.

pronunciation.title: Ending ts, and a soft hl
pronunciation.text: «C» in «moc» is «ts». «H» is breathy: «tohle» is TOH-hleh with no vowel between «h» and «l». The final «é» is long. Stress: first syllable.

translations.en-GB: Do you have it in blue too?
translations.en-US: Do you have it in blue too?
translations.bg-BG: Имате ли го и в синьо?
translations.pl-PL: Czy macie to też w niebieskim?

mnemonic.title: Modrý: a moody blue
mnemonic.text: «Modrý» (blue) sounds like “moody”: picture a moody blue sky. Czech also has «světle modrý» (light blue).

grammar.title: Colours change with the noun
grammar.text: «Modrý» (masc.), «modrá» (fem.), «modré» (neut.). After «v» the colour takes the locative: «v modré» (in blue). «I» means “too, also”.

pronunciation.title: A light rolled r
pronunciation.text: Roll the «r» lightly: «modré». The final «é» is long. «I» alone, between words, is a short «ih» that attaches to the next word: «i v» sounds like “ihv”.

translations.en-GB: Nice to meet you, I'm Anna
translations.en-US: Nice to meet you, I'm Anna
translations.bg-BG: Приятно ми е, аз съм Анна

mnemonic.title: Těší: “tea-shee”, pleased
mnemonic.text: «Těší» sounds like “tea-she”: picture a handshake over tea. «Těší mě» is the all-purpose “nice to meet you”.

grammar.title: «Těšit» + «mě»: it pleases me
grammar.text: «Těší mě» is literally “it pleases me”, with «mě» (me) as the object. «Já» (I) is optional and adds emphasis: «já jsem Anna» or just «jsem Anna».

pronunciation.title: Ť sounds: «tě» is “tye”
pronunciation.text: «Tě» is a soft «tye»: «t» and «y» glide together. «Mě» is «mnyeh». «Jsem» is «sem» (the «j» is nearly silent). Stress: first syllable.

translations.en-GB: I'm here for the first time
translations.en-US: I'm here for the first time

mnemonic.title: Poprvé: pop, first
mnemonic.text: «Poprvé» (for the first time) shares «prv-» with «první» (first). Hook: “pop in” the very first time.

grammar.title: No “am” needed with places
grammar.text: «Jsem tu» means “I am here”: «tu» is “here”, a short form of «tady». «Poprvé» is an adverb, so it never changes. For the second time: «podruhé».

pronunciation.title: «Prv» without a vowel
pronunciation.text: «Jsem» is «sem»: the «j» is almost silent. «Prv» has no vowel: «p-r-v» run together, like Czech «prst» (finger). The final «é» is long. Stress: first syllable of «poprvé».

translations.bg-BG: Аз съм от Англия, а вие?

mnemonic.title: Anglie: Anglia and Anglo
mnemonic.text: «Anglie» (England) is from “Anglia”, the same root as “Anglo-”. Czech writes countries with their own endings: «Německo», «Francie».

grammar.title: «Z» + genitive: where from
grammar.text: «Z» (from) is followed by the genitive. Many country names do not change: «z Anglie». Others do: «z Ameriky», «z Polska». «A vy?» (and you?) returns the question.

pronunciation.title: Z is “z”, and gl is hard
pronunciation.text: The preposition «z» is a buzzing «z». «Gl» is two hard sounds: «ang-gli-ye». «Y» in «vy» sounds like a short «i», not “eye”. Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Mluvím: “mluv” = speak
mnemonic.text: «Mluvím» sounds like “mloo-veem” and belongs to «mluvit» (to speak), like Russian «молвить» (to utter). Picture a mouth moving.

grammar.title: Languages are adverbs
grammar.text: Czech uses a lowercase adverb for a language: «česky» (in Czech), «anglicky» (in English). So «mluvím česky» is simply “I speak Czech”. «Trochu» means “a little”.

pronunciation.title: «Mlu» starts with a cluster
pronunciation.text: Start «mlu-» with «m» and «l» together, no vowel between: «mloo». «Ch» in «trochu» is a throaty «h». «Č» is «ch» as in “church”. Stress: first syllable.

translations.en-GB: Could you speak more slowly, please?
translations.en-US: Could you speak more slowly, please?
translations.bg-BG: Можете ли да говорите по-бавно, моля?
translations.ru-RU: Не могли бы вы говорить помедленнее?

mnemonic.title: Pomaleji: a snail, po-ma-lé
mnemonic.text: «Pomalu» (slowly) is the root of “slow”, like Russian «помалу». Picture a snail: «po-ma-leh-yi», one slow step per syllable.

grammar.title: «-ji» makes it “more”
grammar.text: Adverbs add «-ji» (or «-ěji») for “more”: «pomalu» → «pomaleji» (more slowly), «rychle» → «rychleji» (faster). «Můžete» (you can) takes an infinitive: «mluvit».

pronunciation.title: Long ů, soft ž
pronunciation.text: «Ů» is a long «u» and «ž» is «zh». «Mluvit» begins «ml» with no vowel. «Pomaleji» is five syllables with the stress on the first: PO-ma-le-ji.

mnemonic.title: Dneska: dnes, днес
mnemonic.text: «Dneska» (today) is the casual form of «dnes», the same word as Bulgarian «днес». «Hezky» (nice) is the thing to remember.

grammar.title: Weather with «je» + adverb
grammar.text: Czech describes weather with «je» plus an adverb: «je hezky» (nice), «je zima» (cold), «je horko» (hot). No «it» is needed.

pronunciation.title: «Dn» has no vowel
pronunciation.text: «Dn-» starts with «d» and «n» together: no vowel between. «H» is a light breath. «Y» in «hezky» is a short «i». Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Prší: the sound of rain
mnemonic.text: «Prší» is almost the sound of rain: “pr-shee”, with the «š» hissing like drops on a window. «Venku» means “outside”.

grammar.title: No subject for weather verbs
grammar.text: Weather verbs need no subject: «prší» (it rains), «sněží» (it snows), «fouká» (it’s windy). The verb comes alone, with «venku» for the place.

pronunciation.title: «Prší»: ř after p
pronunciation.text: After «p» the «ř» loses its voice and sounds like a whispered «rsh». Try “p-rsh-ee”. In «venku» the «n» before «k» sounds like «ng».

mnemonic.title: Zima: winter is cold
mnemonic.text: «Zima» means both “winter” and “cold”: the same word as Russian «зима» and Polish «zima». «Je mi zima» is “cold to me”.

grammar.title: Feelings use «mi» (to me)
grammar.text: To say how you feel, Czech uses «je mi» (to me it is): «je mi zima», «je mi horko» (I’m hot), «je mi špatně» (I feel sick). The feeling word sits at the end.

pronunciation.title: Short vowels, soft m
pronunciation.text: «Je mi» runs together: «yeh-mih». «Z» is a buzzing «z». «I» is short, as in “sit”; the stress is on the first syllable: ZI-ma.

translations.en-GB: It's going to rain all day
translations.en-US: It's going to rain all day

mnemonic.title: Celý: whole, целый
mnemonic.text: «Celý» (whole) is the same word as Russian «целый» and Polish «cały»: “the whole day”. «Den» (day) is short and easy.

grammar.title: «Bude» + infinitive: will
grammar.text: The future of an imperfective verb is «bude» + infinitive: «bude pršet» (it will be raining). The same works for «bude foukat» (it will be windy).

pronunciation.title: Czech c is ts
pronunciation.text: «C» in «celý» is «ts», as at the end of “cats”. The final «ý» is long. The stress is on the first syllable of each word.

mnemonic.title: Slunečno: sun in it
mnemonic.text: «Slunečno» (sunny) comes from «slunce» (sun): hear “sun” hidden in «slun-». Picture a sun on a hot day.

grammar.title: «-o» makes the weather word
grammar.text: Weather words end in «-o»: «horko» (hot), «slunečno» (sunny), «zataženo» (overcast). «A» means “and”. The same pattern: «je teplo» (it’s warm).

pronunciation.title: «č» and a stress on first
pronunciation.text: «Č» is «ch» as in “church”. «Slunečno» has three syllables with the stress on the first: SLOO-nech-no. «H» in «horko» is a light breath.

mnemonic.title: Dělat: “dye-lat”, to do
mnemonic.text: «Dělat» (to do, make) sounds like “dye-lat”: dye something and you’ve made it. Russian «делать» is the same word.

grammar.title: «-š» is informal “you”
grammar.text: Present endings tell the person: «děláš» is “you do” to a friend; to be polite say «děláte». Czech uses the present for plans in the near future too: «co děláš večer?».

pronunciation.title: «Co» is “tso”
pronunciation.text: «Co» begins with a «ts»: «tso». «Dě» is a soft «dye»; the «á» is long. «Č» in «večer» is «ch». Stress: first syllable of each word.

translations.en-GB: Shall we go for a beer?
translations.en-US: Shall we go for a beer?

mnemonic.title: Pivo: “pee-vo”, beer
mnemonic.text: «Pivo» (beer) is almost the same in Russian, Polish and Bulgarian («пиво»). A word that is truly Slavic: easy to remember.

grammar.title: Perfective verbs mean “will”
grammar.text: «Půjdeme» is the future of «jít» (to go): the perfective verb needs no «bude». A plain question needs just a rising voice; word order stays.

pronunciation.title: Long ů, and «jd»
pronunciation.text: «Ů» is a long «u»: “oo”. «Jd» is «yd». «Pivo» has a short «i» like in “sit”. Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Sobota: Sabbath
mnemonic.text: «Sobota» (Saturday) comes from the same root as “Sabbath”: the rest day. Bulgarian «събота» and Polish «sobota» match it.

grammar.title: «V» + accusative for days
grammar.text: Days take «v» and the accusative: «v sobotu», «v neděli» (Sunday), «v pondělí». «Mám čas» (I have time) is the everyday way to say you are free.

pronunciation.title: «V» before s sounds like f
pronunciation.text: «V» before a voiceless «s» turns into «f»: «f sobotu». «Č» is «ch». The «á» in «mám» is long. Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Sejdeme: go together
mnemonic.text: «Sejít se» is made of «se-» (together) and «jít» (go): people who “go together” meet. Picture two paths joining.

grammar.title: «Se» means each other
grammar.text: «Se» here means “each other”: «sejdeme se» is “we’ll meet”. «Se» takes the second place in the sentence: «Kdy se sejdeme?».

pronunciation.title: «Kd» sounds like “gd”
pronunciation.text: «K» before «d» becomes voiced: «gd». «Y» in «kdy» is a short «i». «Sejdeme» has stress on the first syllable: SEY-de-me.

translations.en-GB: I can't today, I've got work
translations.en-US: I can't today, I've got work
translations.ru-RU: Сегодня не могу, у меня работа

mnemonic.title: Práce: a long practice
mnemonic.text: «Práce» (work) sounds like “prah-tse”: picture a long practice you can’t skip. Related: «pracovat» (to work).

grammar.title: «Ne-» negates the verb
grammar.text: Glue «ne-» to the front of a verb to negate it: «můžu» → «nemůžu» (I can’t). After «mám» the thing you have is in the accusative: «práce» → «práci».

pronunciation.title: Long á in «práci»
pronunciation.text: «Ů» and «á» are long. «C» is «ts»: «prá-tsi». The negative «ne-» takes the stress: NEH-moo-zhoo. Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Odbavení: sent off
mnemonic.text: «Odbavení» (check-in) is «od-» (off) plus «bavit» (to see to): the place where you’re “seen to” and sent off. Polish says «odprawa».

grammar.title: Nouns in «-ení» are neuter
grammar.text: Many words ending in «-ení» are neuter: «odbavení», «zpoždění», «nádraží». The question form is always «Kde je…?» (where is…?).

pronunciation.title: «Dě» and «ně» are soft
pronunciation.text: «Kde» is «gde». «Ně» is a soft «nye». The long «í» at the end is held a beat. Stress: first syllable: OD-ba-ve-ní.

mnemonic.title: Letadlo: a flying thing
mnemonic.text: «Letadlo» is «let» (flight) plus «-adlo» (a tool for): “a flying tool”. «Zpoždění» sounds like Russian «поздно» (late).

grammar.title: «Mít» + noun for a state
grammar.text: Czech says “has a delay”: «má zpoždění», lit. “has delay”. The same pattern works for «Mám hlad» (I’m hungry) and «Mám strach» (I’m afraid).

pronunciation.title: «zp» sounds like “sp”
pronunciation.text: «Zp» loses its voice and sounds like «sp». «Ž» is «zh». «Dě» is a soft «dye» and «ně» a soft «nye». Stress: first syllable.

translations.bg-BG: Не мога да намеря паспорта си

mnemonic.title: Pas: a pass for borders
mnemonic.text: «Pas» (passport) is a short form of «cestovní pas». It looks like “pass”: a pass to cross borders.

grammar.title: «Svůj»: my own
grammar.text: «Svůj» means “one’s own” and points back to the subject: «Nemůžu najít svůj pas» (my own passport). It avoids confusion with «můj» (my), which is used for the speaker in other positions.

pronunciation.title: «ů» sounds like «oo»
pronunciation.text: «Ů» is a long «u»; «svůj» ends like “sv-ooy”. «J» in «najít» is a short «y». Stress: first syllable of each word.

mnemonic.title: Přímý: a straight line
mnemonic.text: «Přímý» (direct) is a straight line: picture an arrow. Related: «přímo» (straight ahead), as in directions.

grammar.title: Question without a question word
grammar.text: Czech makes a yes/no question by tone alone: «Je to přímý let?» sounds like a statement with a rising end. The adjective comes before the noun and agrees: «přímý let» (masc.).

pronunciation.title: Ř and long ý
pronunciation.text: «Př» is «p» then «rzh»: say both quickly. «Ý» is the same as «í»: «ee», long. Stress: first syllable.

translations.en-GB: Where do I pick up my suitcase?
translations.en-US: Where do I pick up my suitcase?
translations.bg-BG: Къде мога да взема куфара си?

mnemonic.title: Kufr: a coffer
mnemonic.text: «Kufr» (suitcase) is like “coffer”, a box, and German «Koffer». Picture a travel coffer on the belt.

grammar.title: Present of perfective = future
grammar.text: «Vyzvednu» is the perfective: the present form means “I’ll pick up”. «Si» (for myself) comes second in the sentence: «Kde si vyzvednu kufr?».

pronunciation.title: Final consonants
pronunciation.text: «Kufr» ends with a syllabic «r»: say a small «er» sound at the end. «Zv» in «vyzvednu» keeps both sounds. Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Pomoc: help, помощь
mnemonic.text: «Pomoc» (help) sounds like Russian «помощь». «Pomozte» is the polite command from «pomoci» (to help).

grammar.title: Polite command: «-te»
grammar.text: Use «-te» to ask politely: «pomozte», «počkejte» (wait). «Mi» (me) stays short: «Pomozte mi» (help me). Add «prosím» (please) to soften it.

pronunciation.title: «zt» sounds like «st»
pronunciation.text: «Z» before «t» loses its voice: «pomoste». «Prosím» has a long «í». Stress: first syllable of each word.

mnemonic.title: Rozumět: reason
mnemonic.text: «Rozumět» (to understand) is built on «rozum» (reason): to have reason about it. Russian «разум» and Polish «rozum» are the same.

grammar.title: «Ne-» + verb: no space
grammar.text: Czech glues «ne-» to the verb: «rozumím» → «nerozumím». «Promiňte» (excuse me, sorry) is the polite command from «prominout».

pronunciation.title: Soft «ň»
pronunciation.text: «Ň» is a soft «ny», like the «ni» in “onion”. «Promiňte» has stress on the first syllable, and «nerozumím» on the first too: NE-ro-zu-mím.

mnemonic.title: Policie: police
mnemonic.text: «Policie» is “police” with a Czech ending: you already know it. It is the same in Russian «полиция».

grammar.title: «Volat» + accusative
grammar.text: «Volat» (to call) takes the thing called in the accusative: «policie» → «policii». For an emergency, «Volejte!» is short and clear. The number is 158 for police, 112 everywhere.

pronunciation.title: «c» in the middle
pronunciation.text: «C» is «ts»: «poli-tsi-ji». «Ej» is «ey» as in “they”. Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Ztratit: lose a trail
mnemonic.text: «Ztratit» (to lose) sounds like “stra-tit”: picture a stray that has lost its way. Polish «stracić» is the same word.

grammar.title: «Se» for “myself”
grammar.text: «Ztratil jsem se» is “I lost myself”. A woman says «ztratila jsem se». In the past tense, «jsem» follows the verb; «se» takes second place only after it.

pronunciation.title: «zt» is “st”
pronunciation.text: «Z» before «t» loses its voice: «stratil». «Jsem» is «sem»: the «j» is almost silent. Stress: first syllable.

phrases.target: Je tu někdo, kdo mluví anglicky?

translations.en-GB: Is there anyone here who speaks English?
translations.en-US: Is there anyone here who speaks English?
translations.bg-BG: Има ли някой тук, който говори английски?
translations.ru-RU: Здесь есть кто-нибудь, кто говорит по-английски?
translations.pl-PL: Czy jest tu ktoś, kto mówi po angielsku?

mnemonic.title: Někdo: some-who
mnemonic.text: «Někdo» is «ně-» (some-) plus «kdo» (who): “somebody”. Add «ně-» to others: «něco» (something), «někde» (somewhere).

grammar.title: «Kdo» starts a relative clause
grammar.text: «Kdo» (who) joins the two parts: «někdo, kdo mluví…» (someone who speaks…). «Anglicky» is the adverb for “in English”. Notice «je tu» (is here): no «there».

pronunciation.title: «Kd» is “gd”
pronunciation.respelling: YEH too NYEG-do gdo MLOO-vee ANG-glits-kee
pronunciation.text: «Kd» sounds like «gd». «Ně» is a soft «nye». «Mluví» begins «ml» with no vowel. Stress: first syllable of each word.

mnemonic.title: Pracovat: work like a practice
mnemonic.text: «Pracuju» (I work) comes from «práce» (work): think of “practice” you do every day. Polish «pracować» is the same.

grammar.title: «V» + locative: in a place
grammar.text: «V» (in) puts the place in the locative: «kancelář» → «v kanceláři». The ending changes to «-i» for feminine soft nouns. «Pracuju» is the spoken form of «pracuji».

pronunciation.title: «Ř» in «kanceláři»
pronunciation.text: «C» is «ts»; «ř» is «r» and «zh» together. «V» before «k» is «f». The «á» in «kanceláři» is long. Stress: first syllable of each word.

mnemonic.title: Studovat: study
mnemonic.text: «Studovat» is “study” with a Czech ending: the same word as «student». «Univerzita» is “university”, also easy.

grammar.title: «Na» + locative: at
grammar.text: «Na» + locative says where you study: «na univerzitě» (at university). Czech uses «na» for institutions like «na škole» (at school).

pronunciation.title: «Tě» is “tye”
pronunciation.text: «Tě» at the end is a soft «tye». «Y» in the middle is a short «i». The stress is on the first syllable: STU-du-ju.

translations.en-GB: I've got a lot of work today
translations.en-US: I've got a lot of work today

mnemonic.title: Hodně: a hodge-podge heap
mnemonic.text: «Hodně» (a lot) sounds like “hodge-podge”: a heap of things. «Hodně práce» is a heap of work.

grammar.title: «Hodně» + genitive
grammar.text: «Hodně» (a lot of) is followed by the genitive: «hodně práce» (work), «hodně peněz» (money). Here «práce» already looks like its genitive, so it does not change.

pronunciation.title: Soft «ně»
pronunciation.text: «Ně» in «hodně» is «nye». «Á» is long: «prá-ce». Stress: first syllable of each word.

mnemonic.title: Doma: dom + a
mnemonic.text: «Doma» (at home) is «dom» (house, Russian «дом») with an «-a». Picture a laptop on a sofa.

grammar.title: «Doma» or «domů»
grammar.text: «Doma» answers “where?” (at home); «domů» answers “where to?” (home): «jdu domů» (I’m going home). The same split exists for «tady» (here) and «sem» (to here).

pronunciation.title: Short and sweet
pronunciation.text: «C» is «ts»; the «u» is a pure «oo». «Doma» is two syllables, stress on the first: DO-ma.

translations.en-GB: I have a meeting at ten
translations.en-US: I have a meeting at ten

mnemonic.title: Schůzka: a skoos-ka meeting
mnemonic.text: «Schůzka» (a meeting) sounds like “skoos-ka”: “excuse me, I’m in a meeting”. From «scházet se» (to come together).

grammar.title: Times with «v» + number
grammar.text: Hours are given with «v» (at): «v deset» (at ten), «v osm» (at eight). The number does not change. «Mám» (I have) puts the meeting in the accusative: «schůzka» → «schůzku».

pronunciation.title: The ů in «schůzka»
pronunciation.text: «Ch» is a throaty «kh»: «skhoos-ka». «Ů» is a long «u». «V» before «d» keeps its voice: «v deset». Stress: first syllable.

translations.bg-BG: Мога ли да заредя телефона си?

mnemonic.title: Dobít: beat it back to full
mnemonic.text: «Dobít» sounds like “doh-beat”: “beat” the battery back up to full. It is «do-» (up to) + «bít» (to beat).

grammar.title: «Do-» finishes the action
grammar.text: The prefix «do-» means “up to the end”: «dobít» (top up), «dopít» (finish a drink). «Si» means “for myself”, like in «Můžu si…?».

pronunciation.title: Short i, long í
pronunciation.text: «Ů» is a long «u»; «ž» is «zh». «Dobít» has a long «í»: «do-BEET». Stress: first syllable of «dobít» is DO.

phrases.target: Jaké je tu heslo na wifi?

translations.bg-BG: Каква е паролата за вайфая тук?
translations.pl-PL: Jakie jest tu hasło do wifi?

mnemonic.title: Heslo: a «hes» slogan
mnemonic.text: «Heslo» (password, motto) sounds like “hes-low”: a password you keep low-key. It is also the word for “slogan”.

grammar.title: Adjectives agree with «heslo»
grammar.text: «Heslo» is neuter, so «Jaké» ends in «-é»: «Jaké je heslo?» For a feminine noun you would say «Jaká je…?». «Na» + accusative shows what it is for: «na wifi».

pronunciation.title: Wifi is read in Czech
pronunciation.respelling: YAH-keh yeh too HES-lo nah VIH-fih
pronunciation.text: «Wifi» is read the Czech way: «vi-fi». «Jaké» has a long final «é». «H» in «heslo» is a light breath. Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Signál: signal
mnemonic.text: «Signál» is “signal” with an accent: the same word, only the «á» is long. A one-word reminder.

grammar.title: Double negatives are normal
grammar.text: Czech keeps negatives together: «Nemám nic» (I have nothing), «Nikdy nemám signál» (I never have signal). «Ne-» sits in front of «mám»: «nemám».

pronunciation.title: Two long «á»
pronunciation.text: The «á» in «nemám» and «signál» is long. «G» is hard, as in “go”. Stress is first syllable: NE-mám, SIG-nál.

mnemonic.title: Zpátky: back on your heels
mnemonic.text: «Zpátky» (back) comes from «pata» (heel): going back on your heels. Picture stepping back with the phone.

grammar.title: Perfective present = future
grammar.text: «Zavolám» is perfective: it means “I will call (once)”. «Ti» (to you, informal) sits second: «Zavolám ti…». With strangers say «vám»: «zavolám vám».

pronunciation.title: «Zp» sounds like «sp»
pronunciation.text: «Zp» is read «sp»: «spáthy». «Á» is long. «Y» in «zpátky» is a short «i». Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Pošlete: post it
mnemonic.text: «Pošlete» sounds like “post-let”: post a letter, send a message. From «poslat» (to send).

grammar.title: Command + short «mi»
grammar.text: «Pošlete» is the polite command, again with «-te». «Mi» (to me) goes second: «Pošlete mi…». «Zpráva» (message) becomes «zprávu» as the object.

pronunciation.title: Zp is «sp» again
pronunciation.text: «Zprávu» is read «správu»: «zp» becomes «sp». «Á» is long. «Š» is «sh». Stress: first syllable.

translations.en-GB: I have two brothers and a sister
translations.en-US: I have two brothers and a sister
translations.bg-BG: Имам двама братя и една сестра
translations.ru-RU: У меня два брата и сестра

mnemonic.title: Bratr, sestra: brother, sister
mnemonic.text: «Bratr» and «sestra» look like “brother” and “sister”: the same Indo-European roots. Russian «брат» and «сестра» are the same.

grammar.title: «Dva» + plural
grammar.text: Numbers 2–4 are followed by the plural: «dva bratry» (two brothers). The object «sestra» becomes «sestru». For women use «dvě» (two): «dvě sestry».

pronunciation.title: Rolled «r»
pronunciation.text: Roll the «r» lightly in «bratry». «Dv» is two consonants together: «dva». Stress: first syllable of each word.

mnemonic.title: Maminka: a cuddly mum
mnemonic.text: «Maminka» is the cuddly form of «máma» (mum), like “mummy”. The «-inka» ending makes things small and warm.

grammar.title: «To je»: this is
grammar.text: «To je» means “this is” for any person or thing, no matter if singular or plural. «Moje» (my) matches the noun: «moje maminka», «můj táta» (my dad).

pronunciation.title: Soft «ng»
pronunciation.text: In «maminka», «n» before «k» sounds like «ng»: «ming-ka». «J» is a short «y». Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Děti: a little ditty
mnemonic.text: «Děti» (children) sounds like “dyeh-ti”: sing a ditty to them. The singular is «dítě» (child).

grammar.title: «Dvě» for fem./neuter
grammar.text: «Dva» goes with masculine nouns, «dvě» with feminine and neuter: «dvě děti», «dvě sestry». «Děti» is plural, so the adjective agrees: «malé děti».

pronunciation.title: Soft «dě» and «ti»
pronunciation.text: «Dvě» is «dvyeh»: «ě» after «v» gives «ye». «Děti» is «dye-tyi», both soft. Stress: first syllable.

mnemonic.title: Babička: babushka
mnemonic.text: «Babička» is the cuddly «babushka»: the same Slavic word as Russian «бабушка». The «-ička» ending makes it small and warm.

grammar.title: «V» + locative for cities
grammar.text: City names change to the locative after «v»: «Brno» → «v Brně», «Praha» → «v Praze». The verb «bydlet» (to live) does not need «is».

pronunciation.title: Silent vowel in Brno
pronunciation.text: «Brně» has no vowel between «b» and «r»: «b’r-nye». «Č» is «ch». Stress: first syllable.

translations.pl-PL: Jak ma na imię wasza córka?

mnemonic.title: Dcera: a squashed daughter
mnemonic.text: «Dcera» (daughter) is “daughter” squashed: «d-ts-e-ra». Russian «дочь» and Polish «córka» are the same word.

grammar.title: «Jak se jmenuje?»: how is she called
grammar.text: «Jak se jmenuje…?» literally asks “how does she call herself?”: Czech uses the reflexive «se». It works for any name: «Jak se jmenuješ?» (what’s your name?).

pronunciation.title: «Dc» and «jm»
pronunciation.text: «Dc» is read «ts»: the «d» is dropped, «dcera» is «tsera». «Jm» begins «ym» with no vowel. Stress: first syllable.

phrases.target: Chtěl bych se objednat na středu

translations.en-GB: I'd like to book for Wednesday
translations.en-US: I'd like to book for Wednesday
translations.bg-BG: Бих искал да запиша час за сряда
translations.ru-RU: Я хотел бы записаться на среду

mnemonic.title: Objednat: «one» inside
mnemonic.text: «Objednat» holds «jedn-» (from «jeden», one): book one slot. Also means “to order”: «objednat si pizzu».

grammar.title: «Chtěl bych»: I'd like
grammar.text: «Chtěl bych» (man) or «chtěla bych» (woman) is a polite “I would like”. Days of the week take «na» + accusative: «na středu» (for Wednesday), «na pátek» (for Friday).

pronunciation.title: Cluster «chtěl»
pronunciation.respelling: HTYEL bikh seh OB-yed-nat nah STRZHEH-doo
pronunciation.text: «Chtěl» starts with a throaty «kh» then «tye»: «khtyel». «Ř» is «r» and «zh». Stress: first syllable.

translations.en-GB: Do you have a free slot tomorrow?
translations.en-US: Do you have an opening tomorrow?
translations.ru-RU: У вас есть свободное время завтра?

mnemonic.title: Termín: terminal
mnemonic.text: «Termín» (a date or slot) is like “terminal”: the end of a wait. «Zítra» (tomorrow) comes from «zítřek».

grammar.title: Adjectives match gender
grammar.text: «Volný» (free) is masculine because «termín» is masculine. Colours and sizes behave alike: «volný stůl», «volná židle». «Máte…?» is the plain way to ask “do you have…?”.

pronunciation.title: Long «í» twice
pronunciation.text: «Á» and «í» are long. «Volný» ends in a long «ý», the same as «í»: «vol-nee». Stress: first syllable of each word.

translations.en-GB: I need to change my booking
translations.en-US: I need to change my reservation

mnemonic.title: Změnit: swap
mnemonic.text: «Změnit» (to change) comes from «změna» (change): picture a swap. Russian «смена» is the same word.

grammar.title: Two verbs together
grammar.text: «Potřebuju» + infinitive: «potřebuju změnit» (I need to change). The object «rezervace» becomes «rezervaci». The same pattern: «potřebuju zrušit» (I need to cancel).

pronunciation.title: «zm» and «ř»
pronunciation.text: «Zm» keeps both sounds: «zmnyeh-nit». «Ě» after «m» gives «nye». «Ř» is «r» and «zh». Stress: first syllable.

translations.en-GB: I want to cancel my booking
translations.en-US: I want to cancel my reservation

mnemonic.title: Zrušit: rush it out
mnemonic.text: «Zrušit» sounds like “zroo-shit”: rush it out of the calendar. It means “to cancel” or “to abolish”.

grammar.title: «Chci» + infinitive
grammar.text: «Chci» (I want) is more direct than «chtěl bych» (I would like). Both take an infinitive: «Chci zrušit». For politeness, say «Chtěl bych zrušit».

pronunciation.title: «Chci» is “khtsi”
pronunciation.text: «Chci» starts with a throaty «kh» and then «tsi»: «khtsi». «Š» is «sh». Stress: first syllable.

translations.en-GB: I'll be there at half past two
translations.en-US: I'll be there at two thirty
translations.bg-BG: Ще дойда в два и половина

mnemonic.title: Půl: half a pool
mnemonic.text: «Půl» (half) sounds like “pool”: a half-full pool. Think half an hour, not a whole one.

grammar.title: «Půl třetí» is 2:30
grammar.text: Czech says “half to three”: «půl třetí» is 2:30, because the hour is the next one. Russian «половина третьего» does the same. «Přijdu» is perfective: “I’ll come (and arrive)”.

pronunciation.title: Ř after p, long ů
pronunciation.text: «Př» and «tř» both contain the Czech «ř»: «r» and «zh» together. «Ů» is long. Stress: first syllable.

phrases.target: Is there a pharmacy near here?

translations.pl-PL: Czy jest tu w pobliżu apteka?

mnemonic.title: Pharmacy starts like «farm»
mnemonic.text: The «ph» is an «f», so «pharmacy» begins like «farm». Picture a little farm that grows pills. In the US you will also see «drugstore» for a shop that sells medicine and more.

grammar.title: «Is there a…?» asks if something exists
grammar.text: «Is there a pharmacy?» asks whether one exists. Add «near here» to mean close to where you stand. Use «a» before a single, new thing: «a pharmacy».

pronunciation.title: The ph is an f
pronunciation.respelling: iz THAIR uh FAR-muh-see NEER heer
pronunciation.text: The «ph» sounds like «f», and the stress is on the first syllable: FAR-muh-see. Americans pronounce every «r», in «pharmacy», «near» and «here».

phrases.target: Do you have anything for a sore throat?

translations.bg-BG: Имате ли нещо за болно гърло?
translations.ru-RU: У вас есть что-нибудь от боли в горле?
translations.cs-CZ: Máte něco na bolest v krku?

mnemonic.title: «Sore» means it hurts to touch
mnemonic.text: A «sore» spot hurts when you touch or use it: a «sore throat», a «sore back», «sore feet». Say «sore» like «soar» and picture a throat that wants to fly away from the pain.

grammar.title: Americans say «Do you have…?»
grammar.text: In the US you ask «Do you have…?», not «Have you got…?». «Anything» is the normal word in a question, and «for» names the problem the medicine treats: «for a sore throat».

pronunciation.title: Th, then r
pronunciation.ipa: [du ju hæv ˈɛn.i.θɪŋ fɚ ə sɔr θroʊt]
pronunciation.respelling: doo yoo HAV EN-ee-thing fer uh SOR throht
pronunciation.text: In «throat» the tongue touches the teeth for «th», then slides back for «r»: th-r-oat. In «sore» the «r» is clearly heard, and «for» is weak: fer.

phrases.target: I've had a fever since last night

translations.ru-RU: Со вчерашнего вечера у меня температура

mnemonic.title: Saturday Night Fever
mnemonic.text: You may know the film «Saturday Night Fever»: «fever» is a high body temperature. The phrase ends with «last night», so the film's «night» and «fever» come together.

grammar.title: «I've had… since»
grammar.text: For something that began in the past and still goes on, use «I've had…», not «I have… since». «Since» takes a starting point: «since last night», «since Monday». An illness like «fever» takes «a».

pronunciation.title: Fee-ver, not fev-er
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪv hæd ə ˈfi.vɚ sɪns læst naɪt]
pronunciation.respelling: ighv HAD uh FEE-ver sinss last nite
pronunciation.text: The first syllable of «fever» is a long «ee» and carries the stress: FEE-ver. «Night» has a silent «gh» and rhymes with «bite». The final «-er» has an American «r»: ver.

mnemonic.title: Allergic ends with an «ick!»
mnemonic.text: The last syllable of «allergic» is «-jik», so it ends like «ick!». Say «ick!» as if you tasted something you cannot eat. «Peanuts» are «pea» + «nuts», though a peanut grows underground.

grammar.title: Allergic TO
grammar.text: The adjective «allergic» takes «to»: «allergic to peanuts», «allergic to cats». «I'm» is «I am». A food you cannot eat in general has no «the»: just «peanuts».

pronunciation.title: G sounds like j, stress on LER
pronunciation.text: In «allergic» the «g» is a «j» and the stress is on the second syllable: uh-LER-jik. The vowel in LER is the American «er». «Peanuts» is stressed on PEE.

phrases.target: Can I make an appointment with a doctor?

translations.bg-BG: Може ли да си запиша час при лекар?
translations.ru-RU: Можно записаться на приём к врачу?
translations.pl-PL: Czy mogę umówić się na wizytę u lekarza?

mnemonic.title: Appointment: a point in time
mnemonic.text: Hidden inside «appointment» is «point»: you point to a spot on the calendar. An «appointment» is a time agreed in advance with a doctor, a dentist or a hairdresser.

grammar.title: Make an appointment
grammar.text: The verb with «appointment» is «make», not «do»: «make an appointment». Use «an» before a vowel sound: «an appointment». Add «with» and the person: «with a doctor».

pronunciation.title: Doctor: DOK-ter
pronunciation.ipa: [kæn aɪ meɪk ən əˈpɔɪnt.mənt wɪð ə ˈdɑk.tɚ]
pronunciation.respelling: kan igh MAYK un uh-POINT-ment with uh DOK-ter
pronunciation.text: «Appointment» has its stress on POINT, rhyming with «joint». «Doctor» has the stress on DOK, and Americans say the «o» open, like «ah», with an «r» at the end.

phrases.target: I have a reservation for tonight

translations.ru-RU: У меня забронирован номер на сегодня

mnemonic.title: Reserved, like a sign on a table
mnemonic.text: «Reservation» comes from «reserve»: to keep something for you. Think of the little «Reserved» sign on a restaurant table. A hotel keeps a room reserved in your name.

grammar.title: «Have a reservation»
grammar.text: In the US you say «I have a reservation», the plain present. «For tonight» says which night. «A reservation» takes «a» because it is one booking among many.

pronunciation.title: Stress on VAY
pronunciation.respelling: igh HAV uh rez-er-VAY-shun fer tuh-NITE
pronunciation.text: The main stress of «reservation» is on VAY: rez-er-VAY-shun. The ending «-tion» is «shun». «Tonight» is stressed on NITE, and its first syllable is weak: tuh.

mnemonic.title: Break + fast
mnemonic.text: «Breakfast» is «break» + «fast»: you break the fast of the night. A «fast» is a time without food, so the first meal ends it.

grammar.title: «Is… included?»
grammar.text: «Included» is the past participle used as an adjective: «is breakfast included?» means «does the price cover it?». The question just swaps the order: «Breakfast is» becomes «Is breakfast».

pronunciation.title: Brek-fust, in-KLOO-did
pronunciation.text: «Breakfast» is two syllables: the «ea» is a short «e» and the second part is weak, «fust». «Included» is stressed on KLOO, and ends in «-did».

phrases.target: Could you give me a wake-up call at seven?

translations.bg-BG: Може ли да ме събудите в седем часа?
translations.ru-RU: Не могли бы вы разбудить меня звонком в семь?
translations.pl-PL: Czy mogą mnie państwo obudzić telefonem o siódmej?
translations.cs-CZ: Mohli byste mě v sedm vzbudit telefonátem?

mnemonic.title: A phone ringing by the bed
mnemonic.text: Picture a phone ringing next to your bed: that is a «wake-up call». The hotel front desk rings your room at the time you ask for.

grammar.title: «Could you give me…?»
grammar.text: «Could you…?» is a polite request. A «wake-up call» is a noun, so it takes «a»: «give me a wake-up call». For the time use «at»: «at seven».

pronunciation.title: Call rhymes with ball
pronunciation.ipa: [kʊd ju ɡɪv mi ə ˈweɪk ʌp kɔl æt ˈsɛv.ən]
pronunciation.respelling: kud yoo GIV mee uh WAYK-up kawl at SEV-un
pronunciation.text: In «could» the «l» is silent: «kud». «Call» is «kawl», rhyming with «ball». «Wake-up» is stressed on WAYK, and «seven» on SEV.

mnemonic.title: Say A/C
mnemonic.text: Americans shorten «air conditioning» to «A/C», said «ay-see». You will hear and see «A/C» everywhere. «Air» + «conditioning» = making the air a good condition.

grammar.title: «Doesn't» + base verb
grammar.text: With «it», «the air conditioning», «the TV», the negative is «doesn't» + the plain verb: «doesn't work», never «doesn't works». The «-s» is already in «doesn't».

pronunciation.title: Work is werk
pronunciation.text: «Work» is «werk», with the American «er» sound, not «walk». «Doesn't» is «DUZ-unt», and «conditioning» is stressed on DISH.

phrases.target: Can I get a late checkout?

translations.bg-BG: Може ли да освободя стаята по-късно?

mnemonic.title: Check, then out
mnemonic.text: «Checkout» is «check» + «out»: you check the room, then you are out. As a noun it means the moment and the time you leave the hotel.

grammar.title: «Can I get…?»
grammar.text: «Can I get…?» is the everyday American way to ask for something. «Late» is an adjective and comes before the noun: «a late checkout». The noun «checkout» is one word.

pronunciation.title: Checkout: stress on CHECK
pronunciation.respelling: kan igh GET uh LAYT CHEK-out
pronunciation.text: The noun «checkout» is stressed on the first part: CHEK-out. «Late» is «layt», rhyming with «date». In fast speech «get a» runs together: «geh-duh».

phrases.target: Do you have these in a size nine?

translations.ru-RU: У вас есть эти в девятом размере?
translations.pl-PL: Czy macie te w rozmiarze dziewiątym?

mnemonic.title: Size rhymes with nine
mnemonic.text: «Size» and «nine» share the same vowel, «ai», like «eyes» and «mine». Say them together: «size nine», and the phrase has its own little rhyme.

grammar.title: «These» for a pair
