grammar.text: Shoes come as a pair, so we say «these», plural, not «this». Add «in a size nine» for the size you need. In US shoe sizes, a size nine is not the same as in Europe.

pronunciation.title: Size ends in z
pronunciation.ipa: [du ju hæv ðiz ɪn ə saɪz naɪn]
pronunciation.respelling: doo yoo HAV theez in uh SIGHZ nine
pronunciation.text: «Size» ends with a «z», not an «s»: «sighz». «These» is «theez», with the voiced «th» and long «ee». The stress falls on HAV, SIGHZ and NINE.

mnemonic.title: Fit + room
mnemonic.text: «Fitting room» is the room where you check the fit. «Fit» is how clothes sit on you, so a «fitting room» is simply a room for trying on. «Dressing room» is also common in the US.

grammar.title: «Where's» = where is
grammar.text: «Where's» is the short form of «where is» and is how people really speak. The question word comes first, then «is»: «Where's the…?». «The» is used because you mean one particular room in this store.

pronunciation.title: Fitting sounds like fid-ing
pronunciation.text: In American English a «t» between vowels turns into a quick «d» sound, so «fitting» sounds like «FID-ing». The stress is on FIT. «Room» has a long «oo».

translations.bg-BG: Тези панталони са ми много големи

mnemonic.title: Pants means trousers
mnemonic.text: In the US «pants» are trousers, the garment with two legs: picture both legs and the plural. In Britain «pants» can mean underwear, so «trousers» is safer there.

grammar.title: Pants is always plural
grammar.text: «Pants» has two legs, so it is always plural: «these pants are», never «this pants is». «Too» comes before the adjective and means more than you want: «too big».

pronunciation.title: Too, to and two
pronunciation.text: «Pants» has the «a» of «cat». «Too», «to» and «two» all sound the same: «too». Stress the words that carry meaning: PANTS and BIG.

phrases.target: Can I pay with a credit card?

translations.bg-BG: Мога ли да платя с кредитна карта?

mnemonic.title: Credit is a cousin of кредит
mnemonic.text: «Credit» is a close cousin of the Bulgarian and Russian «кредит» and the Polish «kredyt». All come from Latin «credo», «I believe»: the shop believes you will pay.

grammar.title: Pay WITH
grammar.text: Use «with» for the means of payment: «pay with a credit card», «pay with cash». «Can I…?» is the normal way to ask permission, and the plain verb follows: «Can I pay».

pronunciation.title: Credit: KRED-it
pronunciation.ipa: [kæn aɪ peɪ wɪð ə ˈkrɛd.ɪt kɑrd]
pronunciation.respelling: kan igh PAY with uh KRED-it KARD
pronunciation.text: «Credit» is stressed on KRED and the «i» is short: KRED-it. In «card» the American «r» is clearly heard. «Pay» is «pay», rhyming with «day».

mnemonic.title: Sale sounds like sail
mnemonic.text: «Sale» sounds like «sail». Picture the price sailing down. Look for red signs saying «Sale» in shop windows: they tell you things cost less.

grammar.title: On sale vs. for sale
grammar.text: In the US «on sale» means the price is reduced, while «for sale» means it can be bought at all. Learn the pair: «Is this on sale?» asks about a discount. «This» points to one item.

pronunciation.title: On is ahn
pronunciation.text: Americans say the «o» of «on» open, like «ah»: «ahn». «Sale» is «sayl», with a long «a» like «day». Stress THIS and SALE, and let «on» be quick.

phrases.target: Nice to meet you. I'm Mike

translations.bg-BG: Приятно ми е. Аз съм Майк
translations.pl-PL: Miło mi cię poznać. Jestem Mike

mnemonic.title: Meet is two hands meeting
mnemonic.text: Picture a handshake: two hands «meet». The word «meet» is exactly what people do the first time. Say it with a smile and a short handshake.

grammar.title: Nice to meet you
grammar.text: «Nice to meet you» is for the first time. Later, say «Nice to see you». After «to» comes the plain verb: «to meet». For your name say «I'm» + name: «I'm Mike».

pronunciation.title: Meet is long, to is weak
pronunciation.respelling: NIGHSS too MEET yoo. ighm MIGHK
pronunciation.text: «Meet» has a long «ee», unlike short «mit». In fast speech «to» becomes weak, «tuh», and «meet you» can blend into «MEE-chew». «Mike» rhymes with «bike».

mnemonic.title: Live like a lively street
mnemonic.text: Picture a «lively» street around your door: «live» is where your life happens. «Around here» draws a circle on the map with you in the middle.

grammar.title: Questions with «do»
grammar.text: A question in the present simple starts with «do»: «Do you live…?», not «You live…?». The verb stays plain: «live», never «lives» after «you».

pronunciation.title: Short i in «live»
pronunciation.text: The verb «live» has a short «i», as in «sit», not the long «eye» of the adjective «live music». «Around» starts with a weak «uh».

phrases.target: What do you do for a living?

mnemonic.title: Living is how you live
mnemonic.text: «Making a living» means earning the money you live on. So «What do you do for a living?» asks what job pays your bills. It is a normal small-talk question in the US.

grammar.title: Two do's, two jobs
grammar.text: The first «do» is the helper that forms the question. The second «do» is the main verb, «to do». Together: «What do you do?». «For a living» makes it clear you mean work.

pronunciation.title: Living with a short i
pronunciation.ipa: [wʌt du ju du fɚ ə ˈlɪv.ɪŋ]
pronunciation.respelling: WUT doo yoo DOO fer uh LIV-ing
pronunciation.text: In «living» the «i» is short, «liv», not «leev». «Do you» flows into «dyoo» or «joo». «For a» is weak: «fer-uh». Stress WHAT, DO and LIV.

mnemonic.title: Vacation: leave it vacant
mnemonic.text: «Vacation» is linked to «vacate» and «vacant»: you leave your desk empty. The word for a trip is «vacation» in the US, where Britons say «holiday».

grammar.title: On vacation, no article
grammar.text: Say «on vacation» with «on» and no «a» or «the»: «I'm on vacation», «I'm here on vacation». Americans say «holiday» mostly for a special day such as Thanksgiving.

pronunciation.title: Stress on KAY
pronunciation.text: «Vacation» is stressed on KAY: vay-KAY-shun, and the first syllable is «vay», not «vah». The «-tion» is «shun». «Here» rhymes with «near».

phrases.target: Could you say that again, please?

translations.ru-RU: Не могли бы вы повторить, пожалуйста?
translations.pl-PL: Czy może pan to powtórzyć, proszę?

mnemonic.title: Again sounds like a-GEN
mnemonic.text: In American English «again» sounds like «uh-GEN», with the stress on «gen», as if you called your friend Gen. Keep that image and you will say it right.

grammar.title: Could you + plain verb
grammar.text: «Could you…?» is a polite request and is followed by the plain verb: «say», not «to say». «Again» goes at the end, and «please» at the very end softens it.

pronunciation.title: The l in could is silent
pronunciation.respelling: kud yoo SAY that uh-GEN pleez
pronunciation.text: In «could» the «l» is silent: «kud». «Again» is «uh-GEN», rhyming with «pen», not «a-GAYN». «Please» ends with a «z»: «pleez».

mnemonic.title: Eighty? That's Fahrenheit
mnemonic.text: Americans measure the weather in Fahrenheit, not Celsius. Eighty degrees is a warm summer day, about 27 °C. Picture a thermometer stuck on «eighty»: a hot one.

grammar.title: «About» before a number
grammar.text: «About» before a number means «roughly»: «about eighty», «about ten minutes». «It's» is «it is», and «it» is the empty subject English needs for weather: «It's hot», «It's eighty degrees».

pronunciation.title: Eighty: the t is soft
pronunciation.text: In «eighty» the stress is on the first syllable and the middle «t» is soft, almost a quick «d»: AY-dee. Don't say «eight-tee» with a hard «t». «Degrees» stresses GREEZ.

translations.bg-BG: Тази вечер трябва да вали сняг

mnemonic.title: Supposed: a weather report in two words
mnemonic.text: «Supposed to» is how people repeat the forecast: it «is supposed to» snow means «the forecast says so». Picture the weatherman pointing at a snowflake map.

grammar.title: «Is supposed to» + verb
grammar.text: «Is supposed to» + base verb passes on what is expected: «It's supposed to snow», «It's supposed to be cold». «Snow» works as both noun and verb, so no «will» is needed.

pronunciation.title: Supposed: d is quiet
pronunciation.text: In «supposed» the stress is on POHZD, and the end «-ed» sounds like a «d» after «z». Before «to», the words run together: suh-POHZD-too. «Snow» has an «s-n» cluster with no vowel between.

mnemonic.title: Humid: like a wet towel
mnemonic.text: «Humid» belongs to «humidity», the water in the air. Picture hot air that feels like a wet towel on your face. Tip: «humid» describes the air, not the water itself.

grammar.title: «So» makes it stronger
grammar.text: «So» before an adjective means «very, really»: «so humid», «so hot». «Out here» means «outside, where I am». Americans often add «out» to the place: «out here», «out there».

pronunciation.title: Hyoo-mid, with an h
pronunciation.text: Say the «h» in «humid»: HYOO-mid, with the stress on the first syllable. The second syllable is short and quiet: mid. «Out here» runs together: owt-heer.

mnemonic.title: Jacket: a coat for in-between days
mnemonic.text: A «jacket» is lighter than a «coat». Think of a jacket you wear when it's neither warm nor really cold. Bulgarian and Russian «жакет» is a different, smart-wear word.

grammar.title: «Do I need…?»
grammar.text: In a question with «I», use «do» and then the base verb: «Do I need…?», not «Need I…?». «Need» is followed by a noun with «a» for one thing: «a jacket».

pronunciation.title: J as in jump
pronunciation.text: «Jacket» starts with «j» as in «jump», and the stress is on JAK: the vowel is the flat «a» of «cat». The end is a quick, weak «-it». «Need» has a long «ee».

phrases.target: Looks like a storm is coming

translations.pl-PL: Wygląda na to, że nadchodzi burza
translations.cs-CZ: Vypadá to, že se blíží bouřka

mnemonic.title: Storm: a word that looks like its sound
mnemonic.text: «Storm» is short and heavy, like thunder. Think of the «st» as the crack and «orm» as the rumble. It names rain, wind and thunder together.

grammar.title: Short sentences drop «it»
grammar.text: In casual speech Americans leave out «It» at the start: «Looks like…» for «It looks like…». «Is coming» is the present continuous and describes something close in time.

pronunciation.title: Storm: a strong r
pronunciation.respelling: luks like uh STORM iz KUM-ing
pronunciation.text: In «storm» the «r» is clear: stor-m, with the lips slightly rounded. «Coming» is spelled with «o» but sounds like «u»: KUM-ing. Stress falls on STORM and KUM.

phrases.target: Are you free on Saturday night?

translations.bg-BG: Свободен ли си в събота вечер?
translations.pl-PL: Czy jesteś wolny w sobotę wieczorem?

mnemonic.title: Free means no plans
mnemonic.text: «Free» here is not «costs nothing»: it means your time is open. Picture an empty square on a calendar. «Are you free?» is the friendly way to start making plans.

grammar.title: «On» with days, «at» with night
grammar.text: Use «on» with a day: «on Saturday». Then «night» tells the part of the day: «Saturday night». Without «on», «Saturday night» is also fine in casual talk, but «on» is the safe choice.

pronunciation.title: Saturday: the middle t
pronunciation.respelling: ar yoo FREE on SAT-er-day nite
pronunciation.text: «Saturday» is stressed on SAT and has a soft «t» between vowels, almost a quick «d»: SAD-er-day. Americans also say «Sat-er-dee» in quick speech. «Night» rhymes with «light».

translations.bg-BG: Искаш ли да вечеряме тази вечер?

mnemonic.title: Grab: take it quick and easy
mnemonic.text: «Grab» means to take fast, like grabbing a seat. «Grab dinner» sounds relaxed, a plan with no fuss. Think of grabbing a bag and heading out.

grammar.title: Dropping «Do you»
grammar.text: Friends often drop «Do you» and start with «Want to…?». It is a normal, friendly question. For a more careful one say «Would you like to…?». «Tonight» already means «this evening», so no «at».

pronunciation.title: Wanna: two words glue together
pronunciation.text: In fast speech «want to» becomes «wanna»: WAH-nuh. Both forms are fine; write «want to». «Dinner» stresses DIN, and «tonight» stresses NITE.

phrases.target: Let's meet at the mall at six

translations.bg-BG: Да се срещнем в мола в шест
translations.ru-RU: Давай встретимся в торговом центре в шесть
translations.pl-PL: Spotkajmy się w galerii o szóstej
translations.cs-CZ: Sejdeme se v nákupním centru v šest

mnemonic.title: Mall: a town under one roof
mnemonic.text: In the US a «mall» is a big shopping centre with many shops inside. Picture a small town with a roof. Bulgarian «мол» and Polish «mall» come from the same word.

grammar.title: «Let's» + verb, «at» for time and place
grammar.text: «Let's» is «let us»: it proposes a plan, followed by the base verb: «Let's meet». «At» works for both a place («at the mall») and a clock time («at six»).

pronunciation.title: Mall rhymes with call
pronunciation.ipa: [lɛts mit æt ðə mɔl æt sɪks]
pronunciation.respelling: lets MEET at thuh MAWL at SIKS
pronunciation.text: «Mall» has the open «aw» sound and rhymes with «call» and «hall». In fast speech the two «at» are weak: uht. «Six» ends with a clear «ks».

phrases.target: I'm on my way. I'll be there in ten minutes

translations.bg-BG: Тръгнал съм. Ще бъда там след десет минути
translations.ru-RU: Я уже еду. Буду через десять минут
translations.pl-PL: Jadę już. Będę za dziesięć minut
translations.cs-CZ: Už jedu. Budu tam za deset minut

mnemonic.title: On my way: you're already moving
mnemonic.text: «On my way» pictures you on the road. You say it when you have already left. It sounds friendly and reassuring to the person waiting.

grammar.title: «In» + time means «from now»
grammar.text: «In ten minutes» counts from now, so it is future: «I'll be there in ten minutes». «I'll» is «I will». Don't use «after ten minutes» for this.

pronunciation.title: Ten minutes: weak endings
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪm ɑn maɪ weɪ aɪl bi ðɛr ɪn tɛn ˈmɪ.nɪts]
pronunciation.respelling: ighm on migh WAY. ighl bee THAIR in TEN MIN-its
pronunciation.text: «Minutes» has stress on MIN and a weak ending: MIN-its. «I'll» sounds like «isle». In «on my way» the stress falls on WAY.

phrases.target: Can we reschedule for next week?

translations.bg-BG: Може ли да пренасрочим за следващата седмица?
translations.pl-PL: Czy możemy przełożyć na przyszły tydzień?
translations.cs-CZ: Můžeme to přesunout na příští týden?

mnemonic.title: Re + schedule = schedule again
mnemonic.text: «Re-» means «again»: «rewrite», «redo», «reschedule». «Schedule» is a plan with a time. So «reschedule» is to make a new time. One prefix, a whole family of verbs.

grammar.title: «For» + new time
grammar.text: To move a plan to a new time, use «for»: «for next week», «for Friday». «Can we…?» is a polite way to ask. «Next week» takes no preposition.

pronunciation.title: Schedule begins with sk
pronunciation.respelling: kan wee ree-SKEJ-ool fer nekst week
pronunciation.text: Americans say «schedule» as SKEJ-ool, with «sk» at the start. So «reschedule» is ree-SKEJ-ool, stress on SKEJ. «Next week» runs together: nekst-week.

phrases.target: Which gate does the flight leave from?

translations.pl-PL: Z której bramki odlatuje ten lot?
translations.cs-CZ: Z kterého gate odlétá ten let?

mnemonic.title: Gate: where you go through
mnemonic.text: A «gate» is a door where you board the plane, like a garden gate. In the US you only say «gate» (not «terminal») for the last step. Picture the number above the door.

grammar.title: Which + noun, then do-question
grammar.text: «Which» + a noun asks you to choose: «which gate», «which flight». After it, the question uses «does» for «the flight»: «does the flight leave». The preposition «from» goes at the end.

pronunciation.title: Gate: ay, not e
pronunciation.ipa: [wɪtʃ ɡeɪt dʌz ðə flaɪt liv frʌm]
pronunciation.respelling: wich GAYT duz thuh FLIGHT leev frum
pronunciation.text: «Gate» has the long «ay» sound, like «late». «Flight» has a silent «gh» and rhymes with «night». «Leave» has a long «ee» and ends in «v».

phrases.target: I have one carry-on and one checked bag

translations.bg-BG: Имам един ръчен багаж и един чекиран куфар
translations.ru-RU: У меня один ручной багаж и один сдаваемый чемодан
translations.pl-PL: Mam jeden bagaż podręczny i jedną walizkę do nadania
translations.cs-CZ: Mám jedno příruční zavazadlo a jedno odbavené

mnemonic.title: Carry on = carry on board
mnemonic.text: You carry it on the plane: «carry» + «on». A «carry-on» is your small bag. A «checked bag» is the one you «check in» and don't see again until the other side.

grammar.title: Counting: one + singular
grammar.text: After «one», the noun stays singular: «one bag», «one carry-on». With two, add «-s»: «two bags». «Checked» is a participle used as an adjective: «a checked bag».

pronunciation.title: Carry-on: stress on the first part
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪ hæv wʌn ˈkæ.ri ɑn ænd wʌn tʃɛkt bæɡ]
pronunciation.respelling: igh HAV wun KAIR-ee on and wun CHEKT bag
pronunciation.text: «Carry-on» is stressed on CARR: KAIR-ee on. «Checked» ends in a «t» sound, not «ed»: chekt. «Bag» has the flat «a» of «cat».

translations.pl-PL: Gdzie jest kolejka do kontroli bezpieczeństwa?
translations.cs-CZ: Kde je fronta na bezpečnostní kontrolu?

mnemonic.title: Line: Americans queue in a line
mnemonic.text: In the US you stand in a «line», not a «queue». Picture a straight line on the floor with people on it. «Security» is the safety check before the gates.

grammar.title: Where's = where is
grammar.text: «Where's» is short for «where is» and is used in speech. With a single thing, use «is»: «Where's the line?». With plural things, use «are»: «Where are the gates?».

pronunciation.title: Security: stress on KYUR
pronunciation.text: «Security» has four syllables with stress on the second: sih-KYUR-ih-tee. The «c» is «k» and the «u» is «yoo». The ending «-ty» has a soft flap «t».

mnemonic.title: Delay: de + lay = put off
mnemonic.text: «Delay» means to put something off: the flight is «laid» later. Picture the plane parked, waiting. The noun is also «a delay»: «a two-hour delay».

grammar.title: Has been + participle
grammar.text: «Has been delayed» is the passive: the flight didn't choose it, something happened to it. «Our flight» is singular, so use «has», not «have». Notice it names the result now.

pronunciation.title: Delayed: two stresses, one on LAYD
pronunciation.text: «Delayed» is stressed on the second syllable: dih-LAYD, and ends with a «d» sound. «Our» is one beat: owr. «Been» is weak: bin.

phrases.target: Excuse me, I think I missed my connection

translations.bg-BG: Извинете, мисля, че изпуснах връзката си
translations.ru-RU: Извините, кажется, я опоздал на пересадку
translations.pl-PL: Przepraszam, chyba spóźniłem się na przesiadkę
translations.cs-CZ: Promiňte, myslím, že jsem zmeškal přípoj

mnemonic.title: Connection: a link between flights
mnemonic.text: «Connection» comes from «connect»: two flights linked by time. Picture a chain: if one link is late, the next one leaves without you. Your fix is calm: ask someone.

grammar.title: «I think» softens
grammar.text: «I think» makes a statement gentler: «I think I missed…». Past simple «missed» fits a finished event. «Excuse me» gets attention before a request. Use it, never «Sorry», for this.

pronunciation.title: Missed: ends in t
pronunciation.ipa: [ɪkˈskjuz mi aɪ θɪŋk aɪ mɪst maɪ kəˈnɛk.ʃən]
pronunciation.respelling: ik-SKYOOZ mee, igh THINK igh MIST migh kuh-NEK-shun
pronunciation.text: «Missed» ends with a «t» sound, not «ed»: mist. «Connection» stresses NEK, and «-tion» sounds like «shun». «Excuse» is a verb here, with a «z» at the end.

mnemonic.title: 911 is nine-one-one
mnemonic.text: In the US the emergency number is «911», said digit by digit: «nine-one-one», never «nine hundred eleven». Picture three quick taps on a phone.

grammar.title: A command, softened by «please»
grammar.text: «Call 911» is a command: the plain verb, with no «you». Adding «please» makes it polite, and it can go at the end.

pronunciation.title: Say each digit
pronunciation.text: «One» is «wun», not «own». «Call» has an open «aw» sound, and the «s» in «please» is a voiced «z».

phrases.target: I'm lost. Can you help me?

translations.bg-BG: Изгубих се. Можете ли да ми помогнете?
translations.ru-RU: Я заблудился. Вы можете мне помочь?
translations.cs-CZ: Ztratil jsem se. Můžete mi pomoct?

mnemonic.title: Lost = loss
mnemonic.text: «Lost» is the past of «lose», and it means you cannot find your way. Picture a «lost and found» box where things wait for their owners.

grammar.title: Two short sentences
grammar.text: Spoken English likes short sentences: «I'm lost.» then a question. «Can you…?» is a polite request, followed by the plain verb: «help me».

pronunciation.title: Open o in lost
pronunciation.respelling: ighm LAWST. kan yoo HELP mee
pronunciation.text: The «o» in «lost» is a long open «aw» for many Americans. Finish with the «st»: lost. In «help» the «l» comes before the «p», so keep your tongue up for a moment.

phrases.target: I locked my keys in the car

mnemonic.title: A locked picture
mnemonic.text: Picture your keys on the seat and the door clicking shut: «lock» is the click. Americans say «car», not «auto», for the everyday vehicle.

grammar.title: Past tense of regular verbs
grammar.text: «Lock» + «-ed» gives the past: «locked». Use «my» for what belongs to you: «my keys». Place goes after «in»: «in the car».

pronunciation.title: Locked ends in t
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪ lɑkt maɪ kiz ɪn ðə kɑr]
pronunciation.respelling: igh LAHKT my KEEZ in thuh KAR
pronunciation.text: After the «k» sound, the «-ed» of «locked» is just a quick «t»: lahkt, one syllable. «Keys» ends in «z». Americans say the «r» of «car» clearly.

mnemonic.title: Someone = some + one
mnemonic.text: «Someone» is «some» + «one»: one person you do not know. Americans often say «somebody» too, with the same meaning.

grammar.title: Is + verb-ing: happening now
grammar.text: «Is following» says it is happening right now: «is» + verb with «-ing». «Someone» takes «is», like «he» or «she». «Me» comes after the verb.

pronunciation.title: Stress SUM and FAH
pronunciation.text: «Someone» is stressed on the first part: SUM-wun. In «following», the «ow» is a long «oh», and the first vowel is open, like «ah»: FAH-loh-ing.

mnemonic.title: Flat as a pancake
mnemonic.text: A «flat» tire is as flat as a pancake: no air in it. Americans spell the wheel part «tire»; the British spell it «tyre», and the sound is the same.

grammar.title: «Got» for what happens to you
grammar.text: In everyday American speech, «I got a…» tells what happened to you: «I got a flat tire», «I got a ticket». «A» comes before the singular noun.

pronunciation.title: Tire = tie + er
pronunciation.text: «Tire» has two sounds in it: «tie» + «er», so it sounds like «TY-er». The «a» of «flat» is the short sound of «cat». American «got» has an open «ah».

phrases.target: I have a conference call at ten

mnemonic.title: A call with a crowd
mnemonic.text: Picture many people sharing one phone line: that is a «conference call». Offices in the US say it all day, and it needs no other word.

grammar.title: «At» for a clock time
grammar.text: Use «at» before a time of day: «at ten», «at noon». Americans say «I have…» for plans and appointments, not «I've got…». Skip «o'clock» when it is clear.

pronunciation.title: Stress KAHN
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪ hæv ə ˈkɑn.fɚ.əns kɔl æt tɛn]
pronunciation.respelling: igh HAV uh KAHN-fer-ents KAWL at TEN
pronunciation.text: «Conference» is stressed on the first syllable, KAHN, with an open vowel. The middle part is weak: fer-ents. Then «call» has the open «aw».

phrases.target: Can you email me the file?

translations.bg-BG: Можеш ли да ми изпратиш файла по имейл?
translations.ru-RU: Можешь отправить мне файл по почте?

mnemonic.title: Email is a verb too
mnemonic.text: «Email» is both a thing (an email) and a verb: «to email someone». The same trick works with «text» and «call», so one word does the whole job.

grammar.title: Verb + person + thing
grammar.text: With «email», «send» and «give», the person comes first and needs no «to»: «email me the file». «Can you…?» opens the request politely.

pronunciation.title: EE-mayl, FILE
pronunciation.respelling: kan yoo EE-mayl mee thuh FILE
pronunciation.text: «Email» is stressed on EE, the long «ee» of «see», and ends in «mayl», like «mail». «File» rhymes with «smile».

phrases.target: I'm taking a day off on Friday

translations.bg-BG: В петък си взимам почивен ден

mnemonic.title: A day that is off
mnemonic.text: A «day off» is a day when work is switched off, like a lamp. Americans «take» a day off, as if lifting it out of the calendar.

grammar.title: Plans with is + -ing
grammar.text: For a plan already arranged, English uses «is» + verb-ing: «I'm taking». Use «on» before a day: «on Friday». The verb with «day off» is «take».

pronunciation.title: Off sounds like awf
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪm ˈteɪ.kɪŋ ə deɪ ɔf ɑn ˈfraɪ.deɪ]
pronunciation.respelling: ighm TAY-king uh DAY AWF ahn FRY-day
pronunciation.text: «Off» has the open «aw»: awf, with a clear «f». «Friday» rhymes with «my day»: FRY-day. «Taking» has the long «ay».

phrases.target: I'll get back to you this afternoon

translations.bg-BG: Ще се свържа с теб следобед
translations.ru-RU: Я свяжусь с вами во второй половине дня
translations.pl-PL: Odezwę się do ciebie po południu

mnemonic.title: Get back = come back to you
mnemonic.text: «Get back to you» is a picture of returning: you will come back to the person with an answer. Useful at work when you need time.

grammar.title: I'll = I will
grammar.text: «I'll» is «I will» and is how English promises something. Say «this afternoon» with no «in» or «at»: «this» does the job.

pronunciation.title: Afternoon: stress NOON
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪl ɡɛt bæk tu ju ðɪs ˌæf.tɚˈnun]
pronunciation.respelling: ighl GET BAK too yoo this af-ter-NOON
pronunciation.text: «Afternoon» is stressed at the end, on NOON, like «noon». The «t» of «get» is soft before «back». «To» is weak: too, or even tuh.

phrases.target: Let's schedule a meeting for Monday

mnemonic.title: Schedule: say «sked»
mnemonic.text: In the US it is «SKED-jool», with a «k» at the start: remember «sked». A «schedule» is the plan of when things happen.

grammar.title: Let's + base verb
grammar.text: «Let's» is «let us» and means «we should»: «Let's schedule…». The verb after it stays plain, with no «to». Use «for» with the day: «for Monday».

pronunciation.title: Schedule starts with sk
pronunciation.respelling: lets SKED-jool uh MEE-ting fer MUN-day
pronunciation.text: In American English «schedule» starts with «sk», not «sh»: SKED-jool. «Meeting» is MEE-ting, and «Monday» is MUN-day, with the «o» as in «sun».

phrases.target: Where can I charge my cell phone?

translations.bg-BG: Къде мога да заредя мобилния си телефон?

mnemonic.title: Cell phone: a phone in a cell
mnemonic.text: In the US a mobile is a «cell phone», or just a «cell». The name comes from «cells», the small areas covered by each tower.

grammar.title: Charge: fill it with power
grammar.text: «Charge» works like charging a battery: you fill it with power. Use «my» for your own thing: «my cell phone». «Where can I…?» is a polite way to ask a place.

pronunciation.title: Charge starts with ch
pronunciation.ipa: [wɛr kæn aɪ tʃɑrdʒ maɪ ˈsɛl foʊn]
pronunciation.respelling: WAIR kan igh CHARJ my SEL fohn
pronunciation.text: «Charge» begins with «ch» and ends in a «j» sound: CHARJ. «Phone» has a long «oh», and its «ph» is an «f».

phrases.target: Can you text me your number?

translations.bg-BG: Можеш ли да ми изпратиш номера си с есемес?
translations.ru-RU: Можешь скинуть мне свой номер сообщением?
translations.pl-PL: Możesz wysłać mi swój numer SMS-em?
translations.cs-CZ: Můžeš mi poslat své číslo esemeskou?

mnemonic.title: Text is a verb
mnemonic.text: In the US you «text» people: the word works as a noun and as a verb, so «text me» means «send me a text message». Americans say «text», not «SMS».

grammar.title: Verb + person + thing
grammar.text: After «text» the person comes first and needs no «to»: «text me your number». «Can you…?» opens a polite request. «Your» goes before the noun.

pronunciation.title: Text ends with kst
pronunciation.respelling: kan yoo TEKST mee yor NUM-ber
pronunciation.text: «Text» ends with a cluster: «k» + «s» + «t», all quick. «Number» is NUM-ber, with the stress first and the «u» as in «sun».

mnemonic.title: A dead battery
mnemonic.text: English says a battery with no power is «dead», as if it stopped breathing. Say it about phones and cars. «Almost dead» is the last bar before it dies.

grammar.title: Almost sits before the adjective
grammar.text: «Almost» means «not quite» and goes before the word it changes: «almost dead». «Is» links «battery» and the state it is in.

pronunciation.title: Battery has three syllables
pronunciation.text: Americans say the «tt» in «battery» as a quick, soft «d»: BAD-er-ee. «Almost» has the open «aw» and a long «oh»: AWL-mohst.

mnemonic.title: Miss like a missed bus
mnemonic.text: You «miss» a call the way you miss a bus: it came and you were not there. In the US a «missed call» also sits in your list as a red mark.

grammar.title: Past tense with -ed
grammar.text: «Miss» + «-ed» gives the past: «missed». The verb takes «your call» as its object: you missed something that was yours to catch.

pronunciation.title: Missed ends with st
pronunciation.text: «Missed» sounds like «mist»: the «ed» is a «t». «Sorry» has an open «ah» for Americans and rhymes with «starry», not «worry»: SAH-ree.

phrases.target: Can you hear me? The connection is bad

translations.bg-BG: Чуваш ли ме? Връзката е лоша

mnemonic.title: Connect, then connection
mnemonic.text: «Connect» means to join, and «connection» is the join itself, like a thread between two phones. A «bad connection» is a thread that keeps breaking.

grammar.title: Hear is not listen
grammar.text: «Hear» is what your ears do by themselves; «listen» takes effort. For a call, ask «Can you hear me?» Use «bad» as the plain opposite of «good».

pronunciation.title: Stress NEK
pronunciation.ipa: [kæn ju hɪr mi ðə kəˈnɛk.ʃən ɪz bæd]
pronunciation.respelling: kan yoo HEER mee thuh kuh-NEK-shun iz BAD
pronunciation.text: In «connection» the stress is on NEK and «-tion» is «shun». The first part is weak: kuh. «Hear» rhymes with «near», and Americans say the «r».

phrases.target: My mom lives close to us

translations.bg-BG: Майка ми живее близо до нас
translations.ru-RU: Моя мама живёт недалеко от нас

mnemonic.title: «Mom» reads the same both ways
mnemonic.text: «Mom» is a palindrome: it reads the same backwards. Picture a hug from both sides. This is the American word; in Britain it is «mum».

grammar.title: «Lives» takes an -s
grammar.text: With «my mom», «he» or «she», the present-tense verb adds «-s»: «lives». «Close to» + a person: «close to us», and after «to» use the object form «us», not «we».

pronunciation.title: Mom is mahm
pronunciation.respelling: migh MAHM livz KLOHSS too uss
pronunciation.text: Americans say «mom» with an open «ah», like «father»: mahm. «Lives» is «livz» with a short «i». The adjective «close» ends in an «s»: klohss.

phrases.target: I have two kids, a boy and a girl

translations.bg-BG: Имам две деца, момче и момиче
translations.ru-RU: У меня двое детей, мальчик и девочка
translations.pl-PL: Mam dwoje dzieci, chłopca i dziewczynkę
translations.cs-CZ: Mám dvě děti, kluka a holčičku

mnemonic.title: A kid is a young goat
mnemonic.text: «Kid» is really a baby goat, and Americans use it for any child: «two kids». It is warm and everyday. Picture two little goats at the playground.

grammar.title: Plural and «a» for each
grammar.text: Two or more things take «-s»: «two kids». A single child takes «a»: «a boy and a girl». In the US «I have…» is the normal way to say it; «I've got…» is more British.

pronunciation.title: Girl is one syllable
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪ hæv tu kɪdz ə bɔɪ ænd ə ɡɝl]
pronunciation.respelling: igh HAV too KIDZ uh BOY and uh GERL
pronunciation.text: «Girl» is a single syllable: gerl, with an «r» sound inside and not «gir-ul». «Kids» ends in a «z». «And» is weak in speech: «un».

mnemonic.title: Husband begins with «house»
mnemonic.text: The old roots of «husband» mean «house-dweller», so think «hus-» = house. The man of the house. Its partner is «wife»: «my wife», «my husband».

grammar.title: Introducing someone
grammar.text: «This is…» introduces one person nearby. Put the name last, after a comma: «my husband, Tom». Use «my» before a family word: «my husband», not «the husband».

pronunciation.title: Husband: HUZ-bund
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable: HUZ-bund. The «s» in «husband» sounds like «z», and the end is soft: «bund», not «band». «Tom» has an open «ah».

phrases.target: My grandma turns eighty next week

translations.bg-BG: На баба ми ѝ стават осемдесет следващата седмица
translations.ru-RU: Моей бабушке на следующей неделе исполнится восемьдесят
translations.pl-PL: Moja babcia kończy w przyszłym tygodniu osiemdziesiąt lat
translations.cs-CZ: Mé babičce bude příští týden osmdesát

mnemonic.title: Grand + ma
mnemonic.text: «Grandma» is «grand» + «ma»: a grand mother. Americans also say «grandpa» for the grandfather. Picture a big cake for a grand occasion.

grammar.title: Turn an age
grammar.text: For a birthday, English says the person «turns» the new age: «turns eighty». A planned future event can use the present tense with a time word: «next week». Note «turns», with an «-s».

pronunciation.title: Eighty: AY-tee
pronunciation.respelling: migh GRAN-mah ternz AY-tee nekst WEEK
pronunciation.text: «Eighty» starts with the same «ay» as «eight»: AY-tee, and the stress is on the first syllable. Don't confuse it with «eighteen», which is stressed on the end. «Turns» has a vowel like «er».

phrases.target: My dad is flying in on Friday

translations.bg-BG: Татко ми пристига със самолет в петък

mnemonic.title: Friday = fry + day
mnemonic.text: Hear «fry» in «Friday» and picture a fry-day: fish frying in a pan. «Fly in» means to arrive by plane, the opposite of «fly out». Think of a plane landing.

grammar.title: Plans: is flying
grammar.text: For a plan already arranged, English uses the present continuous: «is flying in». With a day, say «on»: «on Friday». Americans say «dad», and the phrasal verb «fly in» means to arrive by air.

pronunciation.title: Friday: FRY-day
pronunciation.ipa: [maɪ dæd ɪz ˈflaɪ.ɪŋ ɪn ɑn ˈfraɪ.deɪ]
pronunciation.respelling: migh DAD iz FLY-ing in on FRY-day
pronunciation.text: «Fly» and «Fri» use the same «igh» sound: FLY-ing, FRY-day. Stress the first syllable of both words. «Dad» has the «a» of «cat», short and open.

phrases.target: I'd like to make a reservation for tonight

translations.bg-BG: Искам да направя резервация за тази вечер
translations.ru-RU: Я бы хотел забронировать столик на сегодня вечером
translations.pl-PL: Chciałbym zarezerwować stolik na dzisiaj wieczorem
translations.cs-CZ: Chtěl bych rezervovat stůl na dnes večer

mnemonic.title: Reserve = keep for you
mnemonic.text: «Reservation» comes from «reserve»: to keep something just for you, like a «Reserved» card on a table. In the US restaurants and hotels both say «reservation»; «booking» is more British.

grammar.title: Polite request, then make
grammar.text: «I'd like to…» is the polite way to ask for something: «I'd» = «I would». The verb with «reservation» is «make»: «make a reservation». «For tonight» gives the time.

pronunciation.title: Stress on VAY
pronunciation.ipa: [aɪd laɪk tu meɪk ə ˌrɛz.ɚˈveɪ.ʃən fɔr təˈnaɪt]
pronunciation.respelling: ighd LIKE too MAYK uh rez-er-VAY-shun fer tuh-NITE
pronunciation.text: In «reservation» the main stress is on VAY: rez-er-VAY-shun. The «-tion» is «shun». In «tonight» the stress is on the end: tuh-NITE, and the «gh» is silent.

phrases.target: Do you have any openings on Saturday?

translations.bg-BG: Имате ли свободни места в събота?
translations.ru-RU: У вас есть свободные места на субботу?
translations.pl-PL: Czy macie wolne terminy w sobotę?
translations.cs-CZ: Máte nějaké volné termíny v sobotu?

mnemonic.title: An opening is a gap
mnemonic.text: An «opening» is a free slot, like a door that stands open in a busy schedule. Hairdressers, doctors and restaurants all talk about «openings».

grammar.title: «Any» and a plural
grammar.text: In a question, «any» goes with a plural: «any openings». A day takes «on»: «on Saturday». Americans start with «Do you have…?» for what is available.

pronunciation.title: Opening has three syllables
pronunciation.ipa: [du ju hæv ˈɛn.i ˈoʊ.pə.nɪŋz ɑn ˈsæt.ɚ.deɪ]
pronunciation.respelling: doo yoo HAV EN-ee OH-pun-ingz on SAT-er-day
pronunciation.text: «Opening» is three syllables, with the stress on OH: OH-pun-ing. The ending «-ings» adds a «z». «Saturday» has the stress on SAT, and «-urday» is quick: SAT-er-day.

translations.bg-BG: Резервацията е на името на Джонсън

mnemonic.title: Filed under a name
mnemonic.text: Picture a drawer of folders: the booking is filed «under» the letter «J». That is exactly how English says it: «under Johnson», meaning in that name.

grammar.title: «Under» + the name
grammar.text: «Under» + a surname shows whose name the booking is in. «The reservation» is a specific one, so it takes «the». No «name» needed: say «under Johnson», not «under the name Johnson», in everyday speech.

pronunciation.title: The h in Johnson is silent
pronunciation.text: «Johnson» is «JAHN-sun»: the «h» is silent and the middle «o» is open. «Under» has the stress on UN, with the «u» of «cup». It ends with an American «r».

phrases.target: Can we move it to eight o'clock?

translations.bg-BG: Можем ли да го преместим за осем часа?
translations.pl-PL: Czy możemy przesunąć to na ósmą?
translations.cs-CZ: Můžeme to posunout na osm hodin?

mnemonic.title: O'clock = of the clock
mnemonic.text: «O'clock» is short for «of the clock». Picture a clock striking exactly on the hour. It is only for full hours: «eight o'clock», never «eight-thirty o'clock».

grammar.title: Move it to a time
grammar.text: «Can we…?» asks politely for permission to do something together. «Move it to» + time changes the time: «move it to eight o'clock». «It» replaces the reservation you already mentioned.

pronunciation.title: O'clock: uh-KLAHK
pronunciation.ipa: [kæn wi muv ɪt tu eɪt əˈklɑk]
pronunciation.respelling: kan wee MOOV it too AYT uh-KLAHK
pronunciation.text: «O'clock» is stressed on the end: uh-KLAHK, with an open «ah» like «lock». «Eight» is «ayt», the «gh» is silent. In fast speech «move it» runs together: MOO-vit.

phrases.target: Sorry, I have to cancel my reservation

translations.bg-BG: Съжалявам, трябва да отменя резервацията си

mnemonic.title: The Cancel button
mnemonic.text: You already know «cancel» from the Cancel button on your phone. Same word, same meaning: to stop something that was planned. In Spanish it is «cancelar» too.

grammar.title: Have to = must
grammar.text: «I have to…» says you must do something, and it is softer than «I must». It is followed by the base verb: «have to cancel». Starting with «Sorry» keeps it polite, with no blame.

pronunciation.title: Have to sounds like hafta
pronunciation.ipa: [ˈsɑ.ri aɪ hæv tu ˈkæn.səl maɪ ˌrɛz.ɚˈveɪ.ʃən]
pronunciation.respelling: SAH-ree igh HAF-tuh KAN-sul migh rez-er-VAY-shun
pronunciation.text: In speech «have to» becomes «hafta»: the «v» turns into an «f». «Sorry» in American English is SAH-ree, with an open «ah» (not «sorrow»). «Cancel» is stressed on the first syllable: KAN-sul.
